records.other_names: ginger , jenjibre; jinja (Swahili); a staple of West African,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Ginger traveled the oldest trade routes on earth — out of Asia, across the Indian Ocean on the monsoon dhows, into the Swahili coast and up the Nile, and later throughout the African diaspora, where it became a cornerstone of Caribbean bush medicine. The elders reached for it for the stomach above all: nausea, sluggish digestion, gas, the queasiness of travel and pregnancy. It was warmed into teas for colds and chills and steeped for aches.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nausea (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Ginger is one of the best-studied herbs in the world for nausea. Clinical trials support its use for pregnancy-related nausea, motion sickness, and post-operative and chemotherapy-associated nausea. This is a genuine, human-trial-backed effect. - Digestive comfort (Tier 2 — Promising): Evidence suggests ginger speeds gastric emptying and eases indigestion. - Inflammation & muscle soreness (Tier 2 — Promising): Studies point to modest reductions in inflammation markers and exercise-related soreness.
records.preparation: Fresh root sliced and simmered for tea; grated into food; dried and powdered; candied. A thumb-sized piece of fresh root simmered ten minutes makes a strong cup.
records.cautions: Generally very safe as a food and tea. In large concentrated doses it may thin the blood slightly — relevant if you take blood-thinning medication or face surgery. Pregnant women use it commonly for nausea, but should keep to culinary/tea amounts and mention it to their provider .

records.other_names: turmeric, tumeric; kurkum; the golden root of the spice
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Another traveler of the Indian Ocean trade, turmeric became woven into cooking and healing from East Africa through the diaspora. Traditionally used for joints and swelling, for wounds and skin (as a paste), and for digestion — the golden spice that colored the food and, the elders held, cooled the body’s fires.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Joint discomfort & inflammation (Tier 2 — Promising, edging toward Tier 1): Curcumin, turmeric’s active compound, has been studied in numerous trials for osteoarthritis and inflammatory joint pain, with several showing meaningful benefit. The evidence is genuinely encouraging while still being debated on quality. - The absorption problem (important): Curcumin is poorly absorbed on its own. Traditional cooking solved this by accident — combining turmeric with black pepper (which contains piperine) and with fat/oil dramatically increases absorption. The grandmother’s stew was better pharmacology than a bare capsule.
records.preparation: Cooked into food with pepper and oil; “golden milk” (turmeric simmered in milk with pepper); fresh root grated like ginger .
records.cautions: Culinary amounts are very safe. Concentrated supplements may thin blood, may aggravate gallbladder issues, and can interact with some medications. Rare liver-injury reports exist with high-dose supplements — food amounts are not implicated.

records.other_names: garlic; a remedy recorded on the walls of the Nile
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Garlic appears in the ancient Egyptian medical record, was fed to the pyramid workers for strength, and became a near- universal folk medicine across Africa and the diaspora — for the heart and blood, for colds and infection, for “cleaning” the system.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood pressure (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Multiple trials and reviews find that garlic preparations produce a modest but real reduction in blood pressure, particularly in people who are already hypertensive. Modest is the honest word — a supplement to a heart-healthy life, not a replacement for prescribed medication. - Cholesterol (Tier 2 — Promising): Some evidence of small reductions in total and LDL cholesterol. - Colds (Tier 2 — Promising): Limited evidence suggests garlic may slightly reduce the frequency of colds.
records.preparation: Raw, crushed, and rested ten minutes before eating (this activates allicin, the key compound); cooked into food; aged garlic supplements.
records.cautions: Food amounts are very safe. Concentrated garlic thins the blood — caution with blood-thinning drugs and before surgery. Can cause heartburn and, famously, odor . May reduce the effectiveness of certain HIV medications — a flag worth naming.

records.other_names: hibiscus, roselle, sorrel (Caribbean), bissap(West
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The deep-red drink of a hundred celebrations — bissap in Senegal, zobo in Nigeria, sorrel at Caribbean Christmas. Beyond festivity, the elders used the tart calyces as a cooling drink for the blood and the heart, and for the pressure.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood pressure (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Hibiscus tea has been studied in multiple human trials for mild hypertension and shows a real, if modest, blood-pressure-lowering effect. One of the diaspora’s most beloved drinks turns out to be one of its best-evidenced remedies. - Cholesterol & metabolic markers (Tier 2 — Promising): Some trials suggest improvements in lipid profiles.
records.preparation: Dried calyces steeped in hot water (hot) or cold-brewed, sweetened to taste. The everyday festive drink is the everyday remedy.
records.cautions: Very safe as a drink. May lower blood pressure additively with medication — worth noting if you are already treated for hypertension. Some evidence it may interact with certain drugs (including some for malaria and possibly acetaminophen metabolism). Best avoided in large medicinal quantities during pregnancy.

records.other_names: moringa, the drumstick tree, the horseradish tree, “the
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Cultivated across the Sahel, East Africa, and the tropics, moringa’s leaves, pods, and seeds have long been food-medicine — eaten for strength and nourishment, valued in times of scarcity because the tree gives greens when little else will grow. Nursing mothers took it; the depleted took it.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1 — Research-Supported, as a food): Moringa leaf is genuinely, exceptionally nutrient-dense — protein, vitamins A and C, calcium, iron, potassium. As a whole food fighting nutritional gaps, its value is not in dispute. - Blood sugar & cholesterol (Tier 2 — Promising): Preliminary human and animal studies suggest moringa may modestly support healthy blood sugar and lipid levels. Encouraging, not established. - Anti-inflammatory / antioxidant (Tier 2 — Promising): Rich in active compounds under study.
records.preparation: Fresh leaves cooked like spinach; dried leaf powder in food, drinks, and porridge; pods (drumsticks) in stews.
records.cautions: Leaf and pod, as food, are very safe. The root and root bark should be avoided, especially in pregnancy — they contain compounds that can be harmful. Concentrated extracts may lower blood sugar; mind this if you take diabetes medication.

records.other_names: aloe, sinkle bible (Jamaica); recorded in the
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Among the oldest recorded remedies on earth, aloe appears in the ancient Egyptian medical texts and spread through African and Caribbean healing as the great skin-and-burn plant — the split leaf pressed to a burn, a scrape, a rash — and, as a bitter internal purge, for constipation.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin, burns, wounds (Tier 1/2 — Research- Supported to Promising): The clear inner gel has good evidence for minor burns and skin healing and is widely used for exactly this. Reasonable, well-supported topical use. - Constipation (Tier 2, with a strong caution): Aloe latex — the bitter yellow layer just under the skin — is a powerful laxative. It works, but it is harsh and not for casual use (see cautions).
records.preparation: Topical: the clear inner gel applied directly. Internal (food-grade, decolorized products only): with care.
records.cautions: Do not confuse the gel with the latex. The yellow latex is a harsh stimulant laxative, is not safe for regular use, can cause cramping and electrolyte loss, and oral aloe latex has been flagged as a possible carcinogen — this book does not recommend it. Whole-leaf and latex preparations should be avoided in pregnancy. Topical gel is the safe, well-supported use.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: “Fever grass” names its job: across the Caribbean and West Africa, this fragrant grass was the go-to tea for fevers, colds, and chills, and as a calming, settling drink for the stomach and the nerves at day’s end.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Calm & sleep (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with early support): Widely used as a mild relaxant tea; human evidence is thin but the traditional record is deep and the safety is excellent. - Digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A traditional carminative (gas-easing) tea. - Antimicrobial (Tier 2 — Promising, mostly lab): Lemongrass oil shows antimicrobial activity in the laboratory; this does not yet translate to proven treatment of human infection.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried blades steeped as tea, alone or with ginger; the essential oil for topical/aromatic use only (not to be swallowed).
records.cautions: The tea is very safe. Concentrated essential oil should never be taken internally and should be diluted on skin. Medicinal quantities are best avoided in pregnancy.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with early support

records.other_names: soursop, graviola, guanábana, corossol, sweetsop’s
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The spiny green fruit of the tropics, beloved as food and juice across the Caribbean, West Africa, and Latin America. The leaf was brewed as a calming, sleep-inviting tea; the fruit eaten for nourishment and the digestion.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Calm & sleep (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Soursop leaf tea has a deep traditional record as a mild sedative; formal human evidence is limited. - The cancer question (this book will not dodge it): Soursop is heavily promoted online as a cancer cure. This is Tier “unproven” and carries a serious caution. Laboratory studies have found that certain soursop compounds can kill cancer cells in a dish — but this is true of countless substances that do nothing against cancer in a living body, and there are no human trials showing soursop treats cancer . Do not replace cancer care with soursop. - Serious safety flag — strengthened based on more recent research. Soursop contains annonacin, a documented neurotoxin, and this is the very species at the center of the original Guadeloupe atypical Parkinsonism research. This book’s earlier framing treated the risk as mainly tied to heavy leaf and seed consumption, with the fruit itself safe to enjoy freely — but real chemical analysis has since found meaningful annonacin levels in the fruit pulp and commercial nectar as well, and a 2022 clinical study of 180 Caribbean patients with Parkinsonism found regular , cumulative consumption of Annonaceae fruits — naming soursop specifically — associated with worse disease severity and cognitive impairment. This does not mean occasional soursop as part of a varied diet is established as unsafe for the general population, but “enjoy the fruit freely” is no longer accurate guidance: it is best treated as an occasional fruit rather than a daily staple, with real added caution for anyone with an existing neurological condition or family history of Parkinsonism.
records.preparation: Ripe fruit and juice as an occasional food, not a daily staple; leaf tea only occasionally and in moderation, given the annonacin concern.
records.cautions: Treat both the fruit and the leaf tea as occasional traditional foods rather than daily habits, given annonacin’s presence in the pulp itself and not only the leaf and seed. Avoid concentrated seed/leaf extracts entirely. Not for use in pregnancy. Never use as a substitute for cancer treatment.

records.other_names: bitter melon, bitter gourd, cerasee / cerasee vine
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The bitter vine that grows on Caribbean fences and across African and Asian gardens — brewed as the famous “cerasee tea” for the blood, the “washout” and cleansing, skin troubles, and above all for sugar in the blood. One of the diaspora’s most iconic bitter tonics.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising, with an honest limit): Bitter melon has real biological activity on blood sugar and has been studied in human trials for type 2 diabetes. Results are mixed — some benefit in some studies, not robust enough to call it a proven treatment, and nowhere near strong enough to replace diabetes medication. This is a support-alongside, never- instead-of, situation, and it must be coordinated with a doctor because of additive effects (below). - Traditional cleansing/skin uses (Tier 3 — Traditional Use).
records.preparation: Cerasee tea from the dried vine and leaf (intensely bitter); the fruit cooked as food.
records.cautions: This is a plant that demands a doctor’s involvement if you have diabetes: taken with blood-sugar-lowering medication, it can drive blood sugar too low. Avoid in pregnancy — traditionally associated with pregnancy loss and not safe. Seeds contain a compound that can be harmful to certain individuals. Powerful plant; respect it.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, with an honest limit

records.identity: Chondrus crispus / Genus Gracilaria (often sold as “sea moss”)
records.other_names: sea
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A staple of Caribbean coastal life, sea moss was blended into drinks (“Irish moss” drink), used as a thickener and a strength- and-vitality tonic, and reputed as an aphrodisiac and a nourishing food for the depleted and the recovering. Dr . Sebi elevated it to near-legendary status, which is why it belongs in this batch — presented honestly.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 2/3 — as a mineral-rich food): Sea moss is a genuine source of minerals, notably iodine, along with fiber and trace nutrients. As a traditional nourishing food, that record is real. - The bigger claims (Tier “unproven”): Sea moss is marketed today for immunity, thyroid, skin, weight, libido, and more. Direct human clinical evidence for these specific claims is largely absent. It is a nutritious sea vegetable — not the cure-all the internet sells. - The iodine caution is the headline (see below).
records.preparation: Soaked, blended into a gel, added to smoothies and drinks; used as a food thickener .
records.cautions: Iodine is the double edge. Sea moss can be very high in iodine, and both too little and too much iodine harm the thyroid — heavy daily sea moss can deliver iodine far above safe limits and disrupt thyroid function. People with thyroid conditions should be especially careful and involve a doctor . Wild- harvested sea moss can also concentrate heavy metals from seawater — source matters. Enjoy it as an occasional nourishing food, not a daily megadose.

records.other_names: dandelion; a naturalized “weed” carrying old-world
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Woven into African American and Caribbean root medicine as a “spring tonic” and blood cleanser , and into the liver-and-kidney “bitters” tradition generally — the whole plant, root to flower , eaten and brewed.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Diuretic effect (Tier 2 — Promising): Small human studies support a mild, real water-shedding effect from the leaf. - Digestive bitters (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long-standing use as an appetite and digestion aid; limited formal human trials. - Liver support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A cornerstone of root-doctor “liver cleanse” formulas; laboratory evidence of protective activity exists, human trial evidence is thin.
records.preparation: Root roasted as a coffee substitute; leaves eaten as bitter greens or steeped as tea; whole-plant tinctures.
records.cautions: Generally very safe as food. Avoid with known allergy to ragweed- family plants. Can interact with diuretic medications and lithium. Use caution with gallbladder disease (bitters can stimulate bile flow).

records.other_names: burdock; a root-doctor and bush-medicine staple for the
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A classic of both West African-diaspora root medicine and Caribbean bush practice — brewed as a blood and skin tonic, for acne, eczema, and “cleansing,” often alongside sarsaparilla and yellow dock.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin conditions (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for antioxidant activity): Burdock is rich in antioxidant compounds studied in the lab; direct human trials for acne/eczema are limited but the traditional record is long and consistent. - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some preliminary evidence of a mild supportive effect; not a substitute for treatment.
records.preparation: Dried root simmered as a decoction (20+ minutes); root cooked as a vegetable (common in some cuisines); tinctures.
records.cautions: Generally safe as food and tea. Rare allergic reactions (ragweed-family). Mild diuretic and blood-sugar effects — mind interactions with related medications. Avoid concentrated medicinal use in pregnancy.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for antioxidant activity

records.other_names: sarsaparilla; a foundational root of Caribbean and Central
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Long used across the Caribbean and Central America — including in the Honduran Garifuna and mestizo traditions that shaped Dr . Sebi — as a blood tonic, for skin conditions, joint discomfort, and general vitality. Also historically famous as the flavor base of root beer .
records.what_modern_research_says: - Anti-inflammatory & skin (Tier 2 — Promising): Laboratory studies show real anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activity in sarsaparilla’s compounds; direct human clinical trials remain limited. - Joint comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional record for joint and rheumatic complaints.
records.preparation: Dried root simmered as a decoction, often alongside burdock or dandelion; traditional tonic blends.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated. Can mildly affect how the body handles certain drugs processed by the kidneys and liver — worth a doctor’s awareness if you take prescription medication regularly. Avoid in pregnancy without guidance.

records.other_names: stinging nettle; carried into African American herbalism and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used across many healing traditions for the blood, for joint aches, and — once cooked or dried to remove the sting — as a genuinely nourishing green, rich enough in minerals to serve as a tonic food for the depleted and postpartum.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Allergy/hay fever symptoms (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Freeze-dried nettle leaf has real clinical trial support for easing seasonal allergy symptoms. - Joint discomfort (Tier 2 — Promising): Topical nettle and nettle extracts show benefit in some studies for arthritis-related pain. - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely high in iron, calcium, and other minerals once cooked.
records.preparation: Cooked like spinach (this removes the sting); dried leaf tea; freeze- dried capsules for allergy use.
records.cautions: Fresh raw nettle stings on contact — always cook, dry, or otherwise process before consumption. Mild diuretic and blood-sugar-lowering effects — relevant if on related medications. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy (culinary cooked nettle in modest amounts is a different matter , but caution is warranted).

records.other_names: elderberry; adopted widely into
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Though rooted in European folk medicine, elderberry was thoroughly adopted into Black American home-remedy culture — the syrup on the shelf every autumn, the first reach when a cold announced itself.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Cold and flu symptoms (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Multiple human trials support elderberry extract modestly reducing the duration and severity of cold and flu symptoms when taken early. - Immune support generally (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory support for immune-modulating activity.
records.preparation: Cooked syrup (raw berries and unripe parts are toxic — see caution), lozenges, standardized extracts.
records.cautions: Raw or unripe elderberries, and the plant’s leaves, stems, and seeds, contain compounds that can cause nausea and cyanide-related toxicity — the berries must be cooked before use. Commercially prepared syrups are safe when used as directed. Because it can stimulate immune activity, use thoughtfully if you have an autoimmune condition or take immune-suppressing medication — check with your doctor .

records.other_names: neem; carried along the Indian Ocean trade routes
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A pillar of Indian Ayurvedic medicine that traveled the monsoon trade winds into East Africa, where it took root literally and figuratively — used for the skin, for wounds, as a mouth and dental aid (chewed as a stick), and against parasites.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin & antimicrobial use (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory and some clinical evidence supports neem’s antimicrobial and skin-soothing properties, particularly topically. - Dental use (Tier 2 — Promising): Some clinical evidence supports neem-based products for gum health.
records.preparation: Topical oil and leaf preparations for skin; neem-based dental products; leaf tea used sparingly in some traditions.
records.cautions: Neem oil taken internally, especially in concentrated form, can be seriously toxic — particularly to infants and children — and is not recommended for internal use. Topical use is generally safe for adults but should be patch-tested. Avoid internal use entirely in pregnancy; even topical use should be discussed with a doctor during pregnancy.

records.other_names: kola nut, “the nut of West Africa”; ọ̀bì
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Deeply woven into West African social and spiritual life — offered in welcome, chewed for energy and focus, used ceremonially in Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa custom alike. A natural stimulant that predates coffee’s arrival in the region by centuries in daily use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Stimulant / alertness effect (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Kola nut’s caffeine and related compounds have well-established stimulant effects on alertness and mild fatigue — this is straightforward, well- documented pharmacology. - Digestive aid (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Traditionally chewed to aid digestion after meals.
records.preparation: Chewed fresh or dried; ground into drinks and tonics (kola nut is the historical namesake ingredient of early cola beverages).
records.cautions: Contains real caffeine — mind total stimulant intake, sleep effects, and heart palpitation risk in sensitive individuals. Can raise blood pressure mildly and interact with heart medications and MAOIs. Best limited or avoided in pregnancy and by those with anxiety, insomnia, or heart rhythm concerns.

records.other_names: grains of paradise, alligator pepper , guinea
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A West African spice-medicine central to Yoruba, Akan, and neighboring traditions — used in food for warmth and digestion, and ceremonially (the seeds are still offered in some West African rites of welcome and blessing). Historically traded to Europe along the medieval “Pepper Coast” routes before black pepper dominated the trade.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive & metabolic support (Tier 2 — Promising): Laboratory and some animal studies suggest compounds in grains of paradise may support metabolism and digestive comfort; human clinical trials are limited but growing. - Anti-inflammatory activity (Tier 2 — Promising, mostly lab- stage).
records.preparation: Ground into food as a warming spice; occasionally brewed into tea.
records.cautions: Well tolerated as a culinary spice. Limited safety data exists for concentrated medicinal doses — moderation is the wise course, and pregnant women should stick to occasional culinary amounts only.

records.other_names: African basil, efirin (Yoruba), “tea bush,” clove basil
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A Yoruba and broader West African household staple — grown by the doorway, brewed for fever , colds, and stomach upset, used as a wound wash, and cooked into soups as both flavor and medicine.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antimicrobial activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Good laboratory evidence of antimicrobial and antifungal activity in the essential oil; human clinical trials for infection treatment are limited. - Fever & digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A very long, consistent traditional record.
records.preparation: Fresh leaf tea; cooked into soups and stews; leaf juice applied topically to minor wounds in traditional practice.
records.cautions: Culinary and tea use is well tolerated. Essential oil is potent — dilute before any topical use and never take undiluted essential oil internally. A documented finding, not just general caution: this plant has reported abortifacient effects — concentrated or medicinal-strength preparations should be avoided in pregnancy specifically for this reason, not merely as a general precaution; ordinary light culinary seasoning amounts are the reasonable line.

records.other_names: bladderwrack; a seaweed used in Caribbean and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A brown seaweed harvested along Atlantic coastlines, used traditionally for vitality, weight, and — much like sea moss — as a mineral-rich tonic, sometimes blended into the same Caribbean sea-vegetable drinks.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Iodine/thyroid nutrition (Tier 2 — Promising, with a strong caution): Genuinely rich in iodine, which the thyroid needs — but this cuts both ways severely (see below). - The bigger wellness claims (Tier “unproven”): Popularly marketed for weight loss and metabolism; robust human clinical evidence for these claims is lacking.
records.preparation: Dried and powdered into tonics; occasionally cooked as a sea vegetable.
records.cautions: — This is one of the most important caution flags in the book. Bladderwrack’s iodine content is often very high and inconsistent batch to batch, and it can also concentrate heavy metals and arsenic from seawater depending on where it’s harvested. It can seriously disrupt thyroid function in both directions and should generally be avoided by anyone with a thyroid condition, and avoided in pregnancy without direct medical guidance. Source and dosage matter enormously here — this is not a casual daily tonic.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, with a strong caution

records.other_names: chamomile; widely adopted into Caribbean and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A gentle flower brewed for sleep, calm, colic in infants, and digestive upset — one of the most universally trusted teas across cultures, thoroughly folded into diaspora home medicine.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sleep & mild anxiety (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Clinical trials support chamomile extract for mild anxiety and modestly improved sleep quality. - Digestive upset & infant colic (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable evidence, including some pediatric studies, for mild digestive relief.
records.preparation: Dried flowers steeped as tea; extracts and tinctures.
records.cautions: Very safe for most people. Allergy risk for those sensitive to ragweed- family plants. May mildly potentiate blood thinners. Generally considered low- risk in moderate tea amounts, but check with a provider during pregnancy and before surgery.

records.other_names: peppermint; a digestive staple across African, Caribbean,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used everywhere it grows for the stomach — nausea, gas, cramping — and for headache when rubbed on the temples, and as a simple refreshing tea.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Irritable bowel symptoms (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Enteric-coated peppermint oil has solid clinical trial support for easing IBS symptoms — one of the better-evidenced botanical treatments in this book. - Tension headache (Tier 2 — Promising): Topical diluted peppermint oil on the temples shows some benefit in trials.
records.preparation: Leaf tea; enteric-coated capsules (for IBS, medical-grade products are best); diluted oil applied topically.
records.cautions: Tea is very safe. Undiluted essential oil should never be applied to the face of infants or young children (risk of breathing spasm) and should always be diluted for topical use. Can worsen acid reflux/heartburn in some people. Avoid peppermint oil capsules if you have gallstones.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used as a throat and mouth remedy, a digestive aid, and — separately from its herbal medicinal use — carrying deep spiritual and cleansing significance in various diaspora practices, a dual identity this book keeps distinct and honest about.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sore throat (Tier 2 — Promising): Sage-based throat sprays and gargles show reasonable evidence for symptom relief. - Memory & cognitive function (Tier 2 — Promising): Some human trials suggest mild short- term cognitive benefits; early-stage research.
records.preparation: Leaf tea and gargle; culinary use in cooking.
records.cautions: Culinary and moderate tea use is safe. Sage contains thujone, which in very high concentrated doses (not culinary tea amounts) can be neurotoxic — avoid concentrated sage oil or high-dose extracts, especially in pregnancy and with seizure disorders.

records.other_names: mullein; adopted into African American Appalachian
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The classic “lung leaf” of Southern and Appalachian root medicine, brewed for coughs, congestion, and chest complaints, and used topically for skin and ear troubles.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory/cough support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long, consistent traditional record; direct modern human trials are limited, though the plant’s mucilage content plausibly soothes irritated throats.
records.preparation: Dried leaf and flower tea (always strained well — see caution); traditional ear-oil preparations.
records.cautions: Mullein leaf has fine hairs that can irritate the throat if not strained thoroughly through a fine cloth or coffee filter before drinking. Generally well tolerated otherwise. Limited safety data in pregnancy — use with caution and provider awareness.

records.other_names: guinea hen weed, anamu, mucura; a Caribbean and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Deeply used across the Caribbean and into Central and South America — for pain, inflammation, colds, and as a general strengthening tonic — with a garlic-like scent that gives it several of its names.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Anti-inflammatory & pain (Tier 2 — Promising): Laboratory studies show genuine anti-inflammatory and pain-modulating compounds; human clinical trials remain limited. - The “cancer herb” reputation (unproven — flagged directly): Like soursop, guinea hen weed carries an online reputation as a cancer treatment based on laboratory cell-death studies. No human clinical trials support this use, and it must never substitute for medical cancer care.
records.preparation: Leaf and root tea; tinctures in traditional use.
records.cautions: Should be avoided in pregnancy — has traditional use as an abortifacient in some folk practice, which is itself a safety flag, not a recommendation. A documented finding: the plant contains low concentrations of coumadin-like blood-thinning compounds, so it should be avoided by anyone with a blood-clotting disorder or taking blood-thinning medication, and mentioned to a doctor before any surgery. Limited modern safety data overall; use in moderation and avoid combining with other strong-acting herbs without guidance.

records.other_names: cat’s claw, uña de gato; a Central/South American vine
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A woody vine traditionally used for joint pain, digestive troubles, and as an immune-supporting tonic across Central and South American healing traditions.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Joint discomfort/rheumatoid symptoms (Tier 2 — Promising): Several small human trials suggest benefit for joint pain and inflammation, though larger confirmatory trials are still needed. - Immune support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence).
records.preparation: Dried bark/root decoction; standardized extracts and capsules.
records.cautions: Should be avoided by anyone with autoimmune conditions or on immune-suppressing medication without medical guidance, since it may stimulate immune activity. Avoid in pregnancy — traditional use includes contraceptive/abortifacient application, a clear safety flag. May interact with blood pressure and blood-thinning medications.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence

records.other_names: hydrangea root, seven barks; a Southern and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally as a kidney and urinary tonic — for stones and urinary discomfort — within the Southern root-doctor tradition that Black healers shaped and carried for generations.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Kidney/urinary support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional record; modern human clinical evidence is very limited.
records.preparation: Dried root decoction; tinctures.
records.cautions: — Stronger than this book’s earlier caution suggested. Hydrangea contains a cyanogenic glycoside (hydrangin), and all parts of the fresh plant are genuinely toxic — this is not a minor footnote. Properly dried, prepared root only, and even then: reference sources specify no more than about 2 grams of dried root at a time, and not for extended periods — this is a short-term remedy in traditional use, not a daily tonic. Not recommended in pregnancy. Anyone with existing kidney disease should consult a doctor before use, given the plant’s traditional action on the kidneys.

records.other_names: cascara sagrada (“sacred
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Bark used as a laxative for constipation, valued for generations as a “gentler” plant laxative compared to harsher purgatives.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Laxative effect (Tier 2 — Promising mechanism, weaker clinical evidence than originally believed): Cascara’s stimulant action on the colon is real and pharmacologically well understood — its cascarosides and emodin genuinely increase intestinal motility. However , on closer review: the U.S. FDA ruled in 2002 that nonprescription cascara laxative products were no longer “generally recognized as safe and effective,” citing insufficient supporting evidence, and a 2010 systematic review found no clinically important results from randomized controlled trials in adults with chronic constipation. This is a real correction to this book’s original claim — the mechanism is genuine, but rigorous modern clinical trial support for cascara specifically is weaker than this book first stated. - The important limit remains: Even setting the above aside, stimulant laxatives of this kind are meant for short-term, occasional use only.
records.preparation: Dried, aged bark (fresh bark is too harsh and must be aged at least a year , traditionally) prepared as directed on standardized products.
records.cautions: Not for long-term or daily use — prolonged use can cause dependency for bowel function, electrolyte imbalance, and has been associated with liver concerns in case reports with extended heavy use. Avoid in pregnancy, with existing bowel conditions (like Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis), and avoid combining with other laxatives or diuretics without medical guidance. This is a plant to use occasionally and respectfully, not habitually.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising mechanism, weaker clinical evidence than originally believed

records.other_names: rooibos, “red bush”; a South African tradition entering
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Indigenous to South Africa’s Cederberg region, rooibos was used by the Khoisan and other local peoples long before it became a global export tea — valued as a soothing, everyday drink and for infant colic and skin conditions in South African folk practice.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antioxidant activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Good laboratory evidence of antioxidant compounds; human trials on specific health outcomes are still developing. - Caffeine-free calm (Tier 1, as a simple fact): Naturally caffeine-free, making it a genuinely gentle everyday tea alternative — a modest but real, non-controversial benefit.
records.preparation: Dried leaf and stem steeped as tea, hot or cold.
records.cautions: Very safe for essentially everyone, including children and in pregnancy, as an everyday tea — one of the gentlest entries in this book. Rare reports of interaction with certain liver-metabolized medications in heavy, sustained high- dose use; ordinary tea drinking is not a concern.

records.other_names: baobab, “the tree of life”; found across the African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Nearly every part of the baobab was used traditionally — the fruit pulp for nourishment and fever , the leaves as a vegetable and medicine, the bark for various ailments — earning its “tree of life” name across many African cultures for its role in community survival, especially in dry seasons.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1 — Research-Supported, as a food): The fruit pulp is genuinely exceptional nutritionally — very high in vitamin C, fiber , and antioxidants. This is well-documented and one of the more straightforward, confirmed entries in the book. - Blood sugar/digestive support (Tier 2 — Promising): Some human studies suggest baobab fruit may modestly slow carbohydrate digestion and support steadier blood sugar; encouraging, not conclusive.
records.preparation: Dried fruit pulp powder stirred into water , smoothies, or food; leaves cooked as a traditional vegetable.
records.cautions: The fruit pulp is very safe and food-like. As with any high-fiber addition, introduce gradually to avoid digestive discomfort. No major safety concerns identified for the fruit pulp at food-level use.

records.other_names: bitter leaf, onugbu (Igbo), ewuro (Yoruba), grawa
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: One of West and East Africa’s most trusted bitter greens — cooked into soups (bitterleaf soup is a Nigerian staple) and brewed for the stomach, for fever , and for parasites. Ethiopian tradition (grawa) uses it similarly.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Human and animal studies suggest modest blood-sugar-supportive activity — encouraging but not a replacement for diabetes treatment. - Digestive/antiparasitic use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long, consistent traditional record; some laboratory support for antiparasitic activity.
records.preparation: Leaves washed thoroughly to reduce bitterness, then cooked into soups and stews; occasionally brewed as a bitter tea.
records.cautions: As a cooked food, well tolerated. Concentrated extracts may lower blood sugar — caution with diabetes medication. Traditional use includes fertility- related applications in some regions; avoid concentrated use in pregnancy.

records.other_names: honeybush; South Africa’s sweeter cousin to rooibos
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used by Cape communities in South Africa alongside rooibos, valued as a soothing everyday tea and traditionally for coughs and menopausal complaints.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antioxidant activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory evidence; human trials still developing. - Menopausal comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long traditional record; modern clinical evidence is preliminary.
records.preparation: Dried leaf and stem steeped as tea.
records.cautions: Very safe as an everyday tea, caffeine-free, suitable for most people including in pregnancy in ordinary tea amounts. No major interactions documented.

records.other_names: devil’s claw; a Southern African desert root
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used by San and other Southern African peoples for centuries for joint pain, back pain, and digestive complaints — the root’s distinctive hooked fruit gives the plant its name.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Joint pain / osteoarthritis (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): One of the better clinically studied African botanicals — multiple human trials support meaningful benefit for osteoarthritis and lower back pain.
records.preparation: Dried root decoction; standardized extracts and capsules (the most reliably dosed form given research is largely based on standardized products).
records.cautions: Avoid with stomach ulcers or gallstones (can increase stomach acid). May interact with blood-thinning and blood-sugar medication. Not recommended in pregnancy. Generally one of this book’s better-evidenced entries for joint discomfort specifically.

records.other_names: African ginger , wild ginger , indungulo (Zulu)
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A Southern African relative of true ginger , used in Zulu and other traditional practice for coughs, colds, asthma-related symptoms, and menstrual discomfort. Now critically endangered in the wild due to overharvesting — a sourcing and conservation flag in its own right.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long traditional record; formal human clinical trials are very limited, partly because the plant’s rarity has restricted research access.
records.preparation: Traditionally the rhizome, chewed or prepared as an infusion; increasingly available only through cultivated sources given wild scarcity.
records.cautions: Because wild populations are endangered, this book recommends sourcing only cultivated (not wild-harvested) African ginger — a conservation caution as important as any medical one. Limited modern safety data otherwise; use conservatively. 34B. HONEY (THE OLDEST MEDICINE) Not a plant, but foundational to Part I’s Egyptian record — included here for completeness Names: honey; recorded in the Ebers Papyrus and in healing traditions on every continent Tradition of origin & historical use. Documented in the Egyptian medical papyri as a wound dressing and infection preventative thousands of years before germ theory existed — one of the oldest continuously validated remedies in the human record, and central to African, Caribbean, and diaspora healing traditions alike. What modern research says. - Wound care (Tier 1 — Research-Supported, for acute wounds and burns specifically): Medical-grade honey (particularly manuka and similar high-activity honeys) is used in modern clinical wound care with real evidence behind it for acute wounds and burns — one of the strongest, most literally ancient-to-modern through-lines in this entire book. A real nuance worth naming: the evidence for chronic wounds (such as long-standing venous leg ulcers) is weaker and more mixed — a large randomized trial found no significant benefit over usual care for venous leg ulcers specifically, and at least one wound- care guideline body explicitly does not recommend honey for chronic wound treatment. The strongest evidence supports honey for acute, not chronic, wound care. - Cough (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Clinical trials support honey for easing cough, including in children over one year old. Preparation. Raw or medical-grade honey applied to minor wounds; taken by the spoonful, or in tea, for cough and throat soothing. Cautions. Never give honey to infants under one year old — risk of infant botulism, a serious, well-established safety rule with no exceptions. Otherwise very safe for children and adults. Those with diabetes should account for its sugar content.

records.other_names: grains of Selim, negro pepper , Ethiopian pepper
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A West and Central African spice-medicine used in cooking and traditionally for digestive complaints, respiratory symptoms, and postpartum recovery — often given to new mothers in West African tradition as a warming, restorative spice.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive & antimicrobial activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Laboratory studies support genuine antimicrobial and digestive- supportive compounds; human clinical trials are limited.
records.preparation: Ground pods used as a culinary spice; brewed into postpartum tonic teas in West African tradition.
records.cautions: Well tolerated as a culinary spice. Limited safety data for concentrated medicinal use; postpartum traditional use should be discussed with a midwife or doctor rather than self-directed, particularly regarding dosage. A separate, real finding worth naming: this plant has documented traditional use as a contraceptive in some West African communities, and animal studies have found reproductive-organ effects at concentrated doses — those who are pregnant or trying to conceive should avoid concentrated/medicinal-strength use specifically for this reason, distinct from the postpartum-dosing caution above.

records.other_names: prodigiosa; a Central American and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used in Central American and Caribbean traditional medicine, including the Honduran healing context, primarily for blood sugar support and digestive bitters.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some laboratory and preliminary studies suggest supportive activity; far short of the evidence needed to treat diabetes, and never a substitute for medical care.
records.preparation: Leaf infusion, traditionally bitter .
records.cautions: Limited modern safety data. Anyone with diabetes must involve their doctor before use given the plant’s blood-sugar activity and potential for additive effects with medication. Avoid in pregnancy absent specific medical guidance — safety data is too thin to reassure otherwise.

records.other_names: chaparral, creosote bush
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used in Indigenous North American and adopted into some Central American and diaspora herbal traditions as a tonic and topical remedy. Included here specifically because it appears on so many “detox” and cancer-alternative lists that a comprehensive, honest book cannot leave it out — and because its record is a caution, not an endorsement.
records.what_modern_research_says: - The claims: Chaparral is marketed for cancer , arthritis, and detoxification. - The evidence: there isn’t meaningful human clinical support for these uses, and this is one of the few plants in this book where the caution outweighs any benefit worth listing.
records.preparation: Not recommended by this book for internal use — included for reader awareness rather than as a remedy to prepare.
records.cautions: — This is the strongest caution flag in the entire book. Chaparral has been linked in multiple case reports to serious liver damage and liver failure, serious enough that health authorities in several countries have issued warnings against internal use. This book does not recommend chaparral for internal use under any circumstance. If you encounter it marketed as a cancer or detox remedy, treat that marketing with real skepticism — this is precisely the kind of claim the honesty contract at the front of this book exists to warn you about.

records.other_names: yellow dock; a root-doctor tradition companion to burdock
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Paired traditionally with burdock and sarsaparilla in Southern and Caribbean “blood tonic” formulas, valued especially for iron-deficiency-related tiredness and skin complaints.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Iron-related tiredness (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for a plausible mechanism): The root has a traditional reputation for supporting healthy iron levels; modern trials are lacking, though its traditional pairing with iron-rich foods is a sensible pattern.
records.preparation: Dried root decoction, often blended with burdock and sarsaparilla.
records.cautions: Contains oxalates — those prone to kidney stones should use cautiously and in moderation. Avoid concentrated use in pregnancy. Not a substitute for medical evaluation of significant fatigue or suspected anemia, which deserves bloodwork, not just tea.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for a plausible mechanism

records.other_names: cassia, wild senna, ringworm bush
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used across West Africa and the Caribbean topically for ringworm and skin fungal complaints (the leaves crushed and applied), and the pods traditionally as a laxative, related botanically to standard senna.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical antifungal use (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory evidence for antifungal activity against the skin conditions it’s traditionally used for . - Laxative use (Tier 1 — Research-Supported, short-term only): Senna’s laxative action is well-established pharmacology, same family caution as cascara sagrada.
records.preparation: Fresh leaf crushed and applied topically for skin use; pod preparations for occasional laxative use.
records.cautions: Same laxative-dependency caution as cascara sagrada — short-term use only, not a daily habit. Avoid internal use in pregnancy and with existing bowel conditions. Topical use is generally well tolerated; patch-test first.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: One of Southern Africa’s most widely used medicinal plants — burned, inhaled, and brewed for coughs, colds, fever , and digestive complaints across many Southern African communities, distinct from (though related to) the European wormwood used in absinthe.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory & digestive support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence): Very widely used with a long consistent record; formal human clinical trials remain limited relative to how commonly it is used.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried leaf infusion; steam inhalation for congestion in traditional practice.
records.cautions: Should be avoided in pregnancy — traditional use includes menstrual and labor-inducing applications, a direct safety flag. Avoid prolonged, concentrated use given the wormwood family’s general reputation for neurological effects at high doses (this African species is milder than absinthe wormwood, but caution is still warranted). Not for long-term daily use.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence

records.other_names: black seed, black cumin, habbat al-barakah (“seed of
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used for millennia across North Africa, the Horn, and the Middle East for immunity, digestion, and skin — often called “the seed of blessing” for the breadth of complaints it was trusted to help.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar & blood pressure (Tier 2 — Promising, edging toward Tier 1): A genuinely encouraging and growing body of human trials suggests modest benefit for both markers — one of the better- studied entries in this batch. - Asthma/respiratory support (Tier 2 — Promising): Some clinical evidence supports mild benefit.
records.preparation: Whole or ground seeds in food; cold-pressed oil taken by the spoonful; seed tea.
records.cautions: Generally safe as a food spice. Concentrated oil may lower blood sugar and blood pressure — coordinate with a doctor if you’re on medication for either . Avoid concentrated use in pregnancy.

records.other_names: shea, “women’s gold” — a West African tree whose
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The shea tree’s nuts are processed into shea butter across the West African savanna belt, used for millennia on skin and hair , for wound care, and in infant care — an economic and medicinal cornerstone controlled traditionally by women, a detail worth preserving alongside the plant science.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin moisturizing & minor wound support (Tier 2 — Promising): Good evidence of moisturizing and mild anti-inflammatory benefit for skin; commonly used in modern dermatology-adjacent products for exactly this reason.
records.preparation: Raw or lightly refined butter applied topically.
records.cautions: Very safe for topical use for most people; rare nut-allergy-related sensitivity is possible given its origin as a tree nut product — patch-test if you have tree nut allergies.

records.other_names: tamarind; widespread across Africa, the Caribbean,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used across West Africa, East Africa, and the Caribbean as food, a souring agent, and traditionally for fever , digestive complaints, and as a mild laxative for children in some traditions.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive support (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and some laboratory support for mild laxative and digestive effects. - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in various nutrients and antioxidants as a whole fruit.
records.preparation: Pulp eaten fresh, made into drinks, or cooked into food and sauces.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. High doses of concentrated tamarind may interact with certain pain medications (some evidence it can increase absorption of aspirin-family drugs) — a minor but real flag worth a doctor’s awareness if you take such medication regularly.

records.other_names: guava leaf; a Caribbean and broader tropical remedy
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: While the fruit is beloved as food, the leaf carries its own separate tradition across the Caribbean and Latin America — brewed strong for diarrhea and stomach upset, and used topically for wounds.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Diarrhea (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable body of studies, including some human trials, supports guava leaf extract for reducing diarrhea duration and severity.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried leaf boiled into a strong tea.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated for short-term use. Persistent diarrhea (more than two days in an adult, or any duration with signs of dehydration, blood, or high fever , especially in a child) needs medical evaluation rather than home treatment — guava leaf tea is for mild, brief upset, not a substitute for care when symptoms are serious.

records.other_names: cloves; historically centered on Zanzibar’s
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Zanzibar became one of the world’s great clove-producing centers, and the spice was woven into East African and Swahili coast medicine for tooth pain, digestion, and as an antiseptic.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Dental/tooth pain (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Clove oil’s numbing and antiseptic effect on tooth pain is genuinely well- documented — dentists have used clove oil derivatives (eugenol) for generations. - Digestive support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use).
records.preparation: Whole cloves in cooking; diluted clove oil applied directly to a painful tooth or gum on a cotton swab.
records.cautions: Undiluted clove oil can burn soft tissue — always dilute before topical use, and never give concentrated clove oil to young children. This is not a mild caution: documented cases of children ingesting clove oil have resulted in seizures and serious liver damage requiring hospital treatment. Clove oil also has documented mild blood-thinning activity — anyone on anticoagulant medication like warfarin should mention regular clove oil use to their doctor . Culinary use is very safe. Not a substitute for dental care of an underlying cavity or infection.

records.other_names: yohimbe; a Central/West African tree bark
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Bark used traditionally in Central and West African practice as a stimulant and reputed aphrodisiac, and later extracted into pharmaceutical-grade yohimbine for the same reputation in Western use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Erectile function (Tier 2 — Promising, for the pharmaceutical-grade isolated compound specifically): Prescription yohimbine has some clinical evidence for this use; the crude bark/bark extracts sold as supplements are a different, far less consistent matter .
records.preparation: This book does not provide preparation guidance for raw bark given the safety profile below; where used, it should be as a doctor-supervised pharmaceutical-grade product only.
records.cautions: — One of the more serious caution flags in this book. Yohimbe/ yohimbine can cause significant increases in blood pressure and heart rate, anxiety, and has been linked to serious cardiovascular events in case reports, especially at the inconsistent doses found in unregulated supplements. Anyone with heart disease, high blood pressure, anxiety disorders, or kidney/liver conditions should avoid it entirely, and anyone considering it for any reason should do so only under a doctor’s supervision — this is not a casual bush- medicine entry, and this book includes it specifically so readers encountering it elsewhere understand the real risk. One specific, documented, potentially life- threatening interaction deserves its own mention: combining yohimbe with MAOI antidepressants can be dangerous, and combining it with SSRIs or other antidepressants carries a real risk of serotonin-syndrome-type effects — anyone taking any antidepressant medication should not use yohimbe without their prescriber’s direct involvement.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, for the pharmaceutical-grade isolated compound specifically

records.other_names: African mango, bush mango, dika nut
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Native to West and Central Africa, the seed traditionally used as a food thickener and, in some traditions, for digestive complaints — its modern fame comes almost entirely from Western weight-loss marketing rather than deep traditional medicinal use, and this book says so plainly.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Weight/metabolic markers (Tier 2 — Promising, but marketing has outpaced the science): A small number of human trials suggest modest effects on weight and cholesterol markers; the evidence base is thinner and more mixed than the marketing built around it would suggest.
records.preparation: Seed extract, most commonly encountered as a standardized supplement rather than a traditional home preparation.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated in studied doses. This entry is included partly as a caution against overclaiming — readers should treat aggressive “miracle weight loss” marketing around this plant with real skepticism, consistent with this book’s honesty contract.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, but marketing has outpaced the science

records.other_names: kanna, kougoed; a South African succulent used by
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Traditionally chewed, smoked, or brewed by Khoisan peoples of Southern Africa for mood elevation, stress relief, and to ease hunger and thirst on long journeys — one of the older documented mood-related botanicals on the continent.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Mood & stress (Tier 2 — Promising): A small but genuinely growing body of human research supports mild mood-lifting and anti- anxiety effects, with modern standardized extracts now studied more rigorously than most plants in this book.
records.preparation: Traditionally fermented and chewed, or brewed as tea; modern standardized extracts exist.
records.cautions: Should not be combined with prescription antidepressants (SSRIs/ MAOIs) or other mood-altering medication without medical guidance, given its action on similar pathways in the brain — this interaction caution is genuinely important. Limited safety data in pregnancy.

records.other_names: hoodia; a South African/Namibian desert succulent used
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used for generations by San hunters in the Kalahari to suppress hunger and thirst during long desert treks — a genuinely remarkable piece of traditional ecological knowledge later “discovered” and patented by outside interests without the San people’s early consent or benefit, a case this book flags as part of Part I’s suppression story.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Appetite suppression (Tier “unproven” for commercial products specifically): Despite huge commercial hype in the 2000s weight-loss industry, rigorous human clinical trials have generally failed to confirm meaningful appetite-suppressing effects from the hoodia found in most commercial products, and much of what is sold as hoodia has been found not to contain meaningful amounts of the plant at all.
records.preparation: Traditionally chewed fresh by San communities; not recommended by this book as a prepared home remedy given the weak evidence and quality- control concerns in the commercial market.
records.cautions: Long-term human safety data is limited. This entry is included largely as a caution and a justice note: an extraordinary piece of Indigenous knowledge was commercially exploited without adequate benefit returning to the San people who developed it, and the product it produced does not reliably deliver on its promise.

records.other_names: plantain weed (not the banana-family food plantain) — a
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Widely naturalized and used across African American, Caribbean, and broader folk medicine as an “any weed will do” first- aid plant — leaves crushed and applied fresh to stings, bites, minor cuts, and rashes, often growing right in the yard where it’s needed.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical wound/skin soothing (Tier 2 — Promising, upgraded from traditional-use-only): Long, very consistent traditional first-aid use, real laboratory evidence of anti-inflammatory and wound-healing compounds, and — a genuine update — recent human clinical trials now exist, including a randomized controlled trial on diabetic foot and pressure ulcers and a case-control study on second-degree burn wounds (comparing favorably to standard silver sulfadiazine treatment). This is more human evidence than this book’s traditional-use-only framing had assumed, though the studies remain few in number .
records.preparation: Fresh leaf crushed or chewed into a poultice and applied directly to the skin.
records.cautions: Very safe for topical first-aid use on minor skin irritation. Not a substitute for medical care for a deep wound, an infected bite, or a serious allergic reaction (signs like spreading swelling, difficulty breathing, or fever need a doctor , not a poultice).

records.other_names: okra, gumbo, ladies’ fingers — a plant so central
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Okra crossed the Middle Passage in enslaved cooks’ memory and became a defining ingredient of Southern American and Caribbean cuisine — gumbo takes its very name from a West African word for the plant. Used as food first, and traditionally as a mild digestive soother .
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Several human and animal studies suggest okra may modestly help blood sugar management, likely through its fiber content; encouraging, not a treatment. - Digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for fiber content): Its mucilage is traditionally soothing to the gut; a real, if modest, mechanism.
records.preparation: Cooked as a vegetable; okra water (soaked overnight) is a folk preparation for blood sugar support in some traditions.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. High-oxalate content means those prone to kidney stones should eat in moderation. May have mild additive effects with diabetes medication — worth mentioning to a doctor if eaten in large medicinal quantities rather than ordinary food portions.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for fiber content

records.other_names: cacao, cocoa; a Central/South American and Caribbean
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used ceremonially and medicinally across Mesoamerica long before European contact, and adopted thoroughly into Caribbean and Central American tradition — valued as a heart tonic, mood lifter , and strength-giving food, prepared as a thick, unsweetened drink rather than candy.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Heart & blood vessel health (Tier 1 — Research- Supported, for high-flavanol cacao specifically): Genuinely solid clinical evidence supports flavanol-rich cacao for modest improvements in blood vessel function and blood pressure — one of the better-evidenced plants in this book, provided it’s minimally processed (most commercial chocolate has lost most of the beneficial compounds through processing and added sugar). - Mood (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable evidence for mild mood benefits, separate from its caffeine-like stimulant content.
records.preparation: Raw or minimally processed cacao, traditionally prepared as an unsweetened drink; cacao nibs.
records.cautions: Contains caffeine-family stimulants (theobromine) — mind total intake alongside other stimulants, and limit in pregnancy to modest amounts as one would with caffeine generally. Most benefit is lost in heavily processed, sugared chocolate — this is a food-quality distinction worth being honest about.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 1 — Research- Supported, for high-flavanol cacao specifically

records.other_names: papaya, pawpaw; the fruit is food, but Caribbean tradition
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Beyond the beloved fruit, Caribbean and broader tropical tradition uses the leaf as a meat tenderizer and digestive aid, and the seeds traditionally against intestinal parasites.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive enzymes (Tier 2 — Promising): Papain, the plant’s signature enzyme, has real, well-documented digestive and meat- tenderizing activity; used in some clinical wound-debridement contexts historically. - Antiparasitic seed use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Some laboratory support; human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Ripe fruit as food; young leaf occasionally cooked or brewed (bitter); seeds used sparingly in traditional practice.
records.cautions: Unripe papaya and concentrated leaf/seed preparations should be avoided in pregnancy — traditional use includes labor-inducing applications, a genuine and well-documented safety flag. Ripe fruit as food is safe in pregnancy. Seeds in large quantities may affect fertility in some studies — moderation applies.

records.other_names: annatto, achiote; the red seed that colors Caribbean and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The seed’s red pigment colors countless Caribbean and Latin American dishes, and traditionally the plant was used for skin protection (as a natural sun-shielding paste by some Indigenous groups) and mild digestive complaints.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antioxidant content (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory evidence of antioxidant compounds; specific health- outcome human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Seeds infused in oil for cooking color and flavor; occasionally brewed as a mild tea.
records.cautions: Very safe as a culinary coloring and flavoring. No major interactions documented at food-level use.

records.other_names: sour orange, bitter orange, naranja agria; widely used in
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The leaf (distinct from the fruit peel used elsewhere for weight products) is a Caribbean bush-tea staple for calming nerves and easing sleep, often given to children in mild form for restlessness.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Calm & sleep (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long, gentle traditional record; direct human trials on the leaf tea specifically are limited.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried leaf steeped as a mild tea.
records.cautions: The leaf tea is gentle and widely considered safe, including traditionally for children in modest amounts. This is distinct from bitter orange peel/fruit extracts sold as weight-loss stimulants, which contain synephrine and carry real cardiovascular risk — this book is specifically not endorsing those concentrated extract products, only the traditional mild leaf tea.

records.other_names: avocado leaf; distinct traditional use from the beloved
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: While the fruit is a nutritional staple across the Caribbean and Central America, the leaf carries a separate folk tradition — brewed for cough, digestive complaints, and traditionally for menstrual cramping.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Traditional use (Tier 3): Limited modern human research on the leaf specifically; the fruit’s nutritional benefits (healthy fats, fiber , potassium) are well-established but belong to a food entry, not this medicinal leaf tradition.
records.preparation: Dried leaf steeped as tea.
records.cautions: Generally used in modest traditional amounts; avoid concentrated or frequent use in pregnancy given its traditional association with menstrual/uterine effects. The fruit itself is a very safe food for virtually everyone.

records.other_names: corn silk; adopted into African American Southern folk
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The fine silky threads inside a corn husk, traditionally brewed as a gentle tea for urinary complaints and mild water retention across Southern Black folk medicine and Indigenous American tradition alike.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Mild diuretic effect (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and preliminary scientific support for a gentle water- shedding effect.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried silk steeped as tea.
records.cautions: Very gentle and well tolerated for most people. Those with known allergies to corn should avoid. Mind additive effects if already on diuretic medication.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Native American in origin, echinacea was widely adopted into general American folk medicine, including Black American home-remedy practice, as a cold-and-flu season staple.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Cold prevention/duration (Tier 2 — Promising, genuinely mixed): Research is honestly inconsistent — some trials show modest benefit for shortening colds, others show none. This is one of the more scientifically debated entries in the book, and this book says so rather than overstating either side.
records.preparation: Tea, tincture, or standardized capsules, typically started at the first sign of a cold.
records.cautions: Should be avoided or used cautiously by those with autoimmune conditions, given its immune-stimulating traditional use. Rare allergic reactions in those sensitive to the daisy/ragweed plant family.

records.other_names: fenugreek; entered African and Caribbean
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A staple of Indian Ocean trade cuisine that took deep root in East African and Indo-Caribbean (Trinidad, Guyana) cooking and medicine — used traditionally for milk supply in nursing mothers, blood sugar , and digestive complaints.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): One of the better clinically studied plants in this book — multiple human trials support modest blood-sugar-lowering effects, particularly at mealtime. - Milk supply in nursing mothers (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and some clinical support.
records.preparation: Seeds soaked, cooked into food, or brewed as tea; sprouted seeds eaten as food.
records.cautions: Must be discussed with a doctor if taking diabetes medication, given real additive blood-sugar-lowering effects. Has a distinctive effect on body odor/urine smell that surprises some first-time users (harmless, just worth knowing). Avoid concentrated use in pregnancy beyond ordinary culinary amounts, given some traditional association with uterine stimulation.

records.other_names: watercress; found in Caribbean and West African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A peppery water-growing green eaten across many traditions, including West African and Caribbean market cooking, valued as a blood and vitality tonic food.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely nutrient-dense — vitamin K, vitamin C, and antioxidant compounds; one of the more straightforwardly evidence-backed “superfood” greens. - Antioxidant/cellular support (Tier 2 — Promising): Some laboratory evidence of protective antioxidant activity.
records.preparation: Eaten raw in salads or lightly cooked; juiced.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. Should be sourced from clean, controlled water sources, as wild-harvested watercress can carry parasites from contaminated water — a sourcing caution, not a plant-chemistry one.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Woven into East African, Ethiopian, and Caribbean cooking and medicine alike — for blood sugar , digestion, and warmth — carried along the same monsoon trade routes documented in Part I.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): A genuinely well-studied spice; multiple human trials show modest blood-sugar benefit, particularly after meals. - The distinction that matters: Most cheap “cinnamon” sold commercially is cassia, not true Ceylon cinnamon.
records.preparation: Ground into food and drinks; simmered into tea.
records.cautions: — This is a real, well-documented caution, not a minor footnote. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which in high regular doses can stress the liver , especially relevant for anyone consuming concentrated cinnamon supplements daily. True Ceylon cinnamon contains far less coumarin and is the safer choice for regular higher-dose use. Ordinary culinary sprinkling of either type, occasionally, is not a concern. Diabetics on medication should coordinate cinnamon supplementation with their doctor given its real blood-sugar activity.

records.other_names: cayenne, hot pepper — central to West African,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Hot peppers became inseparable from West African and Caribbean cuisine after their arrival from the Americas, and folk medicine put the same pepper to work — rubbed on aching joints, taken for circulation, and used as a stimulant tonic.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical pain relief (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Capsaicin, the compound that makes peppers hot, has solid clinical evidence for topical pain relief and is used in legitimate medical pain-relief creams for exactly this reason. - Circulation & metabolism (Tier 2 — Promising): Some evidence of mild metabolic and circulatory benefits from regular capsaicin intake.
records.preparation: Cooked into food; topical creams and diluted oils for joint and muscle pain.
records.cautions: Topical capsaicin causes a real burning sensation on first use (normal, fades with repeated use) — always wash hands thoroughly after handling and never touch eyes. Avoid applying to broken skin. High dietary amounts can aggravate acid reflux and ulcers in sensitive individuals. Cayenne has documented mild blood-thinning activity — anyone on blood-thinning medication, or blood pressure medication, should mention regular concentrated cayenne supplement use to their doctor .

records.other_names: ackee; Jamaica’s national fruit, of West African origin,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Brought from West Africa and now inseparable from Jamaican identity and cuisine (ackee and saltfish), used as food first and foremost — this book includes it specifically for a safety reason as much as a culinary one.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food — when properly ripe): A nutritious food when correctly prepared.
records.preparation: Only the ripe, naturally opened (not forced or pried open) arils are eaten, and they must be well cooked.
records.cautions: — One of the most important safety entries in this entire book. Unripe ackee contains hypoglycin, a toxin responsible for “Jamaican vomiting sickness” — a serious, sometimes fatal illness causing severe vomiting and dangerously low blood sugar . Ackee must only be eaten when the pod has opened naturally on the tree, the arils are firm and yellow, the black seeds and pink membrane are discarded, and the flesh is thoroughly cooked. A critical point often misunderstood: cooking does NOT neutralize the toxin in unripe fruit — ripeness, not cooking, is what makes ackee safe. Cooking is still required as standard preparation, but it is not a safeguard against unripe fruit. Never eat ackee that has been forced open, is unripe, or is undercooked, and never reuse water that unripe ackee was cooked in. This is not a rare or exaggerated warning — it is standard, serious food-safety guidance in Jamaica itself.

records.other_names: cassava leaf, manioc leaf — the root is a global
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Across West and Central Africa and the Caribbean, cassava leaf is cooked as a nutrient-dense vegetable (distinct from the starchy root) and traditionally valued for the blood and general nourishment.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 2, as a cooked food): Reasonably nutrient-dense once properly prepared, providing protein and micronutrients the plain root largely lacks.
records.preparation: Leaves must be thoroughly pounded/chopped and cooked at length (traditional preparations often involve extended cooking, sometimes over an hour) before eating.
records.cautions: — A genuine and serious safety flag. Raw cassava leaf, like the raw root, contains cyanogenic compounds that release cyanide and can cause serious poisoning if not properly processed and thoroughly cooked. This is not a plant for casual raw use in any form — traditional, lengthy cooking methods exist precisely because they are necessary, not optional. Always follow proper traditional preparation methods in full.

records.other_names: African potato; a Southern African corm long
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The corm (an underground stem, not a true potato) has deep traditional use across Southern Africa as an immune and general wellness tonic, and gained wider fame in the 1990s and 2000s as an immune- support remedy during the HIV epidemic in the region.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Immune support (Tier 2 — Promising, with a serious caution attached): Some laboratory evidence of immune-modulating compounds; human clinical evidence remains limited and mixed, and it should never be considered a treatment for HIV or any serious immune condition.
records.preparation: Traditionally the corm is dried and prepared as a decoction; this book does not provide detailed preparation guidance given the caution below.
records.cautions: — A genuinely serious flag.
