Case reports and some studies have linked concentrated African potato preparations to liver injury and interference with antiretroviral (HIV) medication, making this an especially important plant to discuss with a doctor before any use, and an especially dangerous one to substitute for actual HIV treatment. This entry exists specifically because the history here is a caution: real people were harmed by exactly this substitution during a real epidemic, and this book will not repeat that mistake.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, with a serious caution attached

records.other_names: locust bean, dawadawa (Hausa), iru (Yoruba) — a
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The fermented seed is a foundational West African seasoning (much like a soy-sauce or miso equivalent in flavor role) and was traditionally valued as a protein-rich, nourishing food, especially important in regions where animal protein was scarce.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as a fermented food): Genuinely protein- and nutrient-rich, and — as a fermented food — plausibly supportive of gut health, in the same general family of benefit as other fermented traditional foods, though specific clinical trials on dawadawa itself are limited.
records.preparation: Fermented seeds used as a seasoning paste or cake in cooking.
records.cautions: Very safe as a traditional fermented food. Can be high in sodium depending on preparation — worth noting for those managing blood pressure.

records.other_names: pumpkin seed, pepitas — used across African,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Seeds saved and eaten as food and traditionally used across many cultures, including West African and Caribbean practice, against intestinal parasites, particularly in children — a genuinely old and widespread use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antiparasitic use (Tier 2 — Promising): Real laboratory evidence supports activity against certain intestinal parasites; modern human clinical confirmation is limited, and this is not a substitute for proper medical deworming treatment where that’s needed and available. - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely nutrient-dense — magnesium, zinc, healthy fats.
records.preparation: Eaten roasted as a snack; ground into food.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. For suspected parasitic infection, especially in a child, medical evaluation and treatment is the appropriate first step — pumpkin seed is a supportive traditional food, not a diagnosis or a cure.

records.other_names: red palm oil; a West and Central African staple distinct
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Unrefined red palm oil has been a West and Central African dietary and medicinal staple for millennia, valued for vitality, wound healing (applied topically), and as a rich cooking fat, long before it became a controversial global commodity crop.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Vitamin A and E content (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely and unusually rich in these nutrients in its unrefined red form — nutritionally distinct from the refined, deep-fry-oil version most Westerners encounter . - Heart health (Tier “****mixed/debated”): Unrefined red palm oil’s saturated fat content is a genuine point of nutritional debate; this book will not overstate a “heart- healthy” claim that the wider research community has not settled.
records.preparation: Used as a traditional cooking oil; applied topically in some traditions for skin and minor wounds.
records.cautions: As with any dietary fat, moderation is reasonable, particularly for those managing cholesterol or heart disease — discuss significant dietary changes with a doctor . This book also flags, separately from health, the well-documented environmental and labor concerns around industrial (not traditional smallholder) palm oil production, worth a conscious consumer’s awareness when sourcing.

records.other_names: breadfruit; a Caribbean and Pacific staple, brought to
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Breadfruit’s introduction to the Caribbean (most famously via Captain Bligh’s voyages) was explicitly a plantation-economics project: a cheap, filling food to feed enslaved laborers at the lowest possible cost to enslavers. That origin does not erase what it became — a genuine staple food embraced and transformed by Caribbean cooking traditions in the centuries since.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition & blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): A nutrient-dense staple carbohydrate; some preliminary research suggests its fiber content may support steadier blood sugar response compared to more refined starches, though it remains a starchy food to be eaten in reasonable portions.
records.preparation: Roasted, boiled, or fried as a staple starch, much like potato or plantain.
records.cautions: A safe, nourishing food for virtually everyone in ordinary portions; those managing blood sugar should treat it like any other starchy staple — a matter of portion, not avoidance.

records.other_names: callaloo (also used regionally for other greens like
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A beloved leafy green across the Caribbean (callaloo) and West Africa, cooked into soups and stews, valued as a nourishing everyday food for the blood and general strength — one of the clearest living examples of the “kitchen pharmacy” this book’s Part III closes on.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in iron, calcium, vitamins A and C, and protein relative to many leafy greens — a real, well-documented nutritional powerhouse.
records.preparation: Cooked into soups, stews, and side dishes, traditionally with onion, pepper , and other aromatics.
records.cautions: Contains oxalates, like many leafy greens — those prone to kidney stones should eat in reasonable variety rather than exclusively. Otherwise very safe and broadly beneficial as a dietary staple.

records.other_names: wild lettuce, “lettuce opium”; adopted into African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Its dried sap was traditionally used as a mild sedative and pain reliever in folk medicine across the American South and beyond — a gentler alternative reached for before stronger options.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sleep & mild pain (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional record; rigorous modern human trials are very limited.
records.preparation: Dried leaf/sap tea; tinctures.
records.cautions: — A real name-correction worth making directly. Despite the “lettuce opium” nickname, wild lettuce contains no actual opioid compounds and does not act on opioid pathways — its sedative and mild pain-relieving compounds (lactucin and related sesquiterpene lactones) work through an entirely different, less-understood mechanism. That said, real caution is still warranted: it should not be combined with sedatives, sleep medication, or alcohol without guidance, and should be avoided in pregnancy and by those with glaucoma. Not for regular daily long-term use without medical guidance. Anyone considering a homemade preparation should be certain of correct plant identification, since misidentification carries real risk.

records.other_names: horsetail; adopted broadly into American and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally as a diuretic and for brittle nails, hair , and connective tissue support, owing to its unusually high natural silica content.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Mild diuretic effect (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and some scientific support. - Hair/nail/connective tissue support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Plausible given silica content; direct human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Dried herb tea; standardized extracts.
records.cautions: Should be avoided in pregnancy and by those with kidney disease, heart conditions, or on diuretic/lithium medication given its real diuretic action. Older , uncultivated horsetail can contain a thiamine-depleting compound — this is a plant for standardized, reputable-source products rather than casual wild foraging.

records.other_names: slippery elm; Native American in origin, thoroughly adopted
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The inner bark’s mucilage was used traditionally to soothe sore throats, coughs, and digestive irritation — one of the gentlest, most trusted “coating” remedies in the American folk tradition.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Throat & digestive soothing (Tier 2 — Promising): The mucilage mechanism is well understood and plausible; direct rigorous human trials are more limited than the plant’s popularity would suggest.
records.preparation: Powdered bark mixed into a gruel or lozenge; tea.
records.cautions: Very safe for most people. Because its mucilage can slow absorption of other things swallowed alongside it, take other medications at a different time from slippery elm preparations. Bark harvesting has raised sustainability concerns for wild elm populations — a sourcing note worth including alongside the safety ones.

records.other_names: comfrey, “knitbone”; widely adopted into diaspora
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Long used topically for bruises, sprains, and healing broken skin — the folk name “knitbone” speaks to its traditional reputation for speeding the mending of injuries.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical use for bruises/sprains (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable evidence supports short-term topical use for these specific complaints.
records.preparation: Topical salve or poultice only, as directed below.
records.cautions: — One of the most important safety flags in this book, alongside chaparral. Comfrey contains pyrrolizidine alkaloids, compounds strongly linked to serious liver damage. Internal use (tea, capsules, tinctures) is not recommended by this book under any circumstance, and even topical use should be short-term (days, not months), applied only to unbroken skin, and avoided entirely in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and in children. Several countries restrict comfrey products for exactly this reason. This is a plant whose traditional reputation is real, but whose safety margin is thin enough to demand real respect.

records.other_names: black walnut hull; a Southern root-doctor tradition remedy
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The green hull surrounding the nut was traditionally used against intestinal parasites and ringworm, and as a topical antifungal wash, within the Southern Black root-doctor tradition.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antiparasitic/antifungal activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Real laboratory evidence of antimicrobial compounds (juglone); direct human clinical trials are limited.
records.preparation: Fresh green hull tincture (traditionally prepared, often dark green- brown and pungent); topical washes.
records.cautions: Juglone, the active compound, is also a known skin irritant and allergen for some people — patch-test topical use. A documented finding: liver toxicity has been reported specifically with concentrated black walnut hull extracts, even though typical traditional doses appear well tolerated short-term — this is a real reason to avoid high-concentration products and long-term use without guidance. Not recommended for internal use in pregnancy or in place of medical treatment for a confirmed parasitic infection. Those with tree nut allergies should exercise real caution given the plant’s origin.

records.other_names: uva ursi, bearberry; adopted into American folk
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Leaves traditionally brewed for urinary tract discomfort, adopted widely into the same Southern and Caribbean-adjacent bush- and-root tradition as hydrangea root and corn silk.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Urinary tract support (Tier 2 — Promising): Some clinical evidence supports short-term use for mild urinary discomfort, largely attributed to its arbutin content, which the body converts to a mild antiseptic compound in the urinary tract.
records.preparation: Dried leaf tea, short-term only (see caution).
records.cautions: Not for long-term or daily use — prolonged use has been associated with liver concern due to hydroquinone-related compounds, and it should be avoided entirely in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and in children. A urinary tract infection with fever , back pain, or blood in the urine needs medical evaluation and likely antibiotics, not herbal tea alone — this plant supports mild discomfort, not a diagnosed infection.

records.other_names: milk thistle; widely adopted into modern diaspora
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: European in origin but thoroughly folded into modern American and Caribbean herbal practice as a go-to liver-support remedy, often recommended alongside burdock and dandelion in “liver cleanse” formulas.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Liver support (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): One of the more rigorously studied plants in this book — silymarin, its active compound, has real clinical trial support for supporting liver health, including in some liver disease contexts, under medical supervision.
records.preparation: Standardized extract capsules are the most reliably dosed form given the research base; seed tea is gentler but less concentrated.
records.cautions: Generally very well tolerated. Those with a ragweed-family allergy should be cautious. Anyone with diagnosed liver disease should use this specifically under a doctor’s guidance rather than alone, precisely because the condition is serious enough to deserve real supervision even when the herb itself is well-evidenced.

records.other_names: wild yam; a Caribbean, Central American, and Southern
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally for menstrual cramping and digestive complaints, and famous as the original plant source from which early progesterone-related pharmaceuticals were chemically derived in a laboratory — a fact regularly, and wrongly, turned into a marketing claim.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Menstrual/digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A reasonable traditional record; direct modern trials are limited. - The “natural hormone” claim (unproven — flagged directly): Wild yam creams and supplements are heavily marketed as delivering natural progesterone or hormone-balancing effects. The human body cannot convert wild yam’s compounds into progesterone on its own — that conversion requires a laboratory process. This is one of the more widespread and persistent overclaims in the modern herbal marketplace, and this book corrects it directly.
records.preparation: Traditional root tea or tincture for its non-hormonal traditional uses.
records.cautions: Reasonably safe in traditional preparations for its traditional (non- hormonal) uses. Avoid relying on wild yam products marketed for hormone balance or menopause as a substitute for actual hormonal healthcare — that marketing claim is not supported by how the body actually processes the plant.

records.other_names: camwood; a West African tree valued for both dye and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The reddish heartwood has long been ground into a cosmetic and ceremonial paste across West Africa (including traditional use on infants’ skin) and used medicinally for skin conditions and as a traditional dye.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional cosmetic and topical record; modern clinical research is very limited.
records.preparation: Ground heartwood mixed into a paste for topical/cosmetic use.
records.cautions: Generally considered safe for topical traditional use; as with any topical wood powder , patch-test for sensitivity, particularly on infant skin, before broader use.

records.other_names: uziza; an Igbo and broader West African pepper spice,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Both the seed (used as a pepper spice) and the leaf (cooked as a vegetable, notably in Nigerian pepper soup) are West African kitchen-medicine staples, valued for warmth, digestion, and postpartum recovery.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive & anti-inflammatory activity (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory evidence of digestive-supportive and anti- inflammatory compounds; human clinical trials are limited.
records.preparation: Ground seed as a culinary spice; leaves cooked into soups.
records.cautions: Very well tolerated as a culinary spice and vegetable. Limited safety data for concentrated medicinal extracts — culinary and traditional food-level use is the safest, best-supported way to use this plant.

records.other_names: sugar apple, sweetsop, custard apple — soursop’s
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Grown and eaten across the Caribbean as a beloved sweet fruit, with the leaf traditionally brewed, much like its soursop relative, as a calming tea.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as fruit): A genuinely nourishing fruit food. - Leaf tea (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with the same family caution as soursop).
records.preparation: Fruit eaten fresh; leaf occasionally brewed as tea, in moderation.
records.cautions: — This caution has been strengthened based on more recent research than a first look at this fruit might suggest. Like soursop, this plant family contains annonacin, a documented neurotoxin. This book’s earlier framing treated the risk as mainly a leaf/seed concern with the fruit safe to “enjoy freely” — but real, more recent research (including direct chemical analysis of fruit pulp, and a 2022 clinical study of 180 Caribbean patients with Parkinsonism) found annonacin present in the fruit pulp itself, and found that regular , cumulative consumption of Annonaceae fruits — including this one by name — was associated with worse disease severity and cognitive impairment in existing Parkinsonism patients. This does not mean occasional fruit as part of a varied diet is unsafe for the general population, but it does mean “eat this freely and without limit” is no longer the right guidance: this fruit is best treated like any other food with a real, if not fully quantified, cumulative-dose consideration — enjoyed in ordinary variety rather than as a daily or primary fruit, especially for anyone with an existing neurological condition or a family history of Parkinsonism. Leaf tea should be treated as occasional, not habitual, exactly as with soursop. Seeds are toxic if crushed and should never be eaten.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with the same family caution as soursop

records.other_names: noni; a Pacific-origin fruit thoroughly adopted into
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally across the Pacific for generations, and picked up enthusiastically by the modern global wellness industry, including within Caribbean and diaspora health culture, as a juice marketed for nearly every ailment imaginable.
records.what_modern_research_says: - The marketing versus the evidence: Noni juice is sold with sweeping wellness claims. The rigorous human clinical evidence for most of these specific claims is thin, and this is a plant where marketing has significantly outpaced science. - Antioxidant content (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory evidence of antioxidant compounds, the most defensible claim available.
records.preparation: Fermented or fresh juice.
records.cautions: Case reports have linked heavy noni juice consumption to liver injury, and its high potassium content is a real concern for anyone with kidney disease or on potassium-affecting medication. This book recommends real skepticism toward sweeping noni marketing claims and moderate use at most.

records.other_names: Madagascar periwinkle; the single most important
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally in Madagascar and parts of the Caribbean for various complaints, but this plant’s true significance is what came after: its compounds became the direct source of vincristine and vinblastine, chemotherapy drugs that transformed survival rates for childhood leukemia and Hodgkin’s lymphoma — one of the most successful plant-to- medicine translations in modern history.
records.what_modern_research_says: - The pharmaceutical derivatives (Tier 1 — Research- Supported, as approved medications): Vincristine and vinblastine are real, FDA- approved, life-saving cancer chemotherapy drugs used in hospitals worldwide. - The raw plant (a direct caution, not a recommendation): This does not mean brewing periwinkle leaf tea at home offers any of this benefit.
records.preparation: This book provides no home preparation guidance for this plant — it is included specifically to tell its story, not to recommend its use outside pharmaceutical medicine.
records.cautions: — This entry exists as a lesson, not a recipe. The raw plant is genuinely toxic in uncontrolled doses, and its real medical power exists only in precisely purified, medically administered pharmaceutical form — never as a home remedy. This is this book’s clearest example of its own thesis: the Architect provided the compound, and He also gave scientists the gift of extracting and purifying it safely. Honoring the plant means honoring both halves of that gift, not skipping the second one.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 1 — Research- Supported, as approved medications

records.other_names: Jamaican dogwood; a genuinely potent Caribbean
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Bark traditionally used across the Caribbean for pain and as a strong sedative — historically potent enough that it was also traditionally used by fishermen to stun fish in enclosed waters, a fact that itself signals real pharmacological strength.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sedative/pain effect (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with real historical pharmacological plausibility): A long traditional record consistent with genuine biological activity; modern rigorous human clinical trials are very limited.
records.preparation: This book does not provide home preparation guidance given the potency and safety profile below.
records.cautions: — A serious caution. Jamaican dogwood is genuinely potent, and improper dosing has real risk of significant sedation, dizziness, and other adverse effects. This is not a casual home tea — traditional use in skilled hands is one thing; unsupervised home use of a plant strong enough to stun fish is another . Anyone considering this plant should do so only under the guidance of an experienced, qualified herbalist, and never combine it with other sedatives, alcohol, or sleep medication.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, with real historical pharmacological plausibility

records.other_names: pimento, allspice; Jamaica’s signature spice
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Central to Jamaican cooking (jerk seasoning’s foundation) and long used medicinally for digestive complaints and, like cloves, for tooth pain, owing to a shared active compound.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Dental/tooth pain (Tier 2 — Promising): Contains eugenol, the same numbing compound found in cloves, giving it real, plausible topical pain-relief activity. - Digestive support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use).
records.preparation: Ground berries in cooking; occasionally brewed as tea; diluted oil for topical tooth pain relief.
records.cautions: Very safe as a culinary spice. As with clove oil, undiluted essential oil should never be used directly on soft tissue or given to young children.

records.other_names: bay rum tree; the source of the classic Caribbean
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Leaves distilled into oil to make traditional “bay rum,” a topical liniment used across the Caribbean for muscle aches, and later adopted into barbershop tradition as a scent and skin tonic.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical muscle relief (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long consistent traditional record for topical application; rigorous modern clinical trials are limited.
records.preparation: Topical liniment, traditionally combined with alcohol as a rub.
records.cautions: For topical use only — not intended for internal consumption; ingestion of the oil is genuinely toxic. Always dilute the essential oil before applying to skin, and patch-test for sensitivity. This oil is high in eugenol (the same compound found in clove), which has documented mild blood-thinning activity — anyone on anticoagulant medication should be aware of this before regular topical use.

records.other_names: star apple, caimito; the leaf carries separate
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: While the fruit is a favorite across the Caribbean, the leaf has a distinct traditional use, brewed as a tea reputed to support blood sugar management.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some laboratory and preliminary studies suggest supportive activity; not established well enough to substitute for diabetes treatment or monitoring.
records.preparation: Dried leaf tea.
records.cautions: Anyone with diabetes should involve their doctor before adding this to a medication regimen, given its blood-sugar activity and the potential for additive effects. A documented animal study found the leaf extract was toxic and even lethal at very high concentrated doses, distinct from the modest amounts used in ordinary traditional tea — a real reason to avoid concentrated extracts or excessive amounts rather than moderate dried-leaf tea. Limited broader safety data otherwise.

records.other_names: taro, cocoyam, dasheen; used in Caribbean callaloo
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Both the root and the broad leaves are staple foods across West Africa and the Caribbean (in some islands, “callaloo” specifically refers to this plant’s leaves rather than amaranth’s), valued for nourishment and as a hearty vegetable.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as a properly cooked food): Genuinely nutrient-dense once properly prepared.
records.preparation: Leaves and root must always be thoroughly cooked — this is not optional.
records.cautions: — A real, important safety flag. Raw taro leaf and root contain calcium oxalate crystals (raphides) that cause significant throat and mouth irritation and are toxic if eaten raw or undercooked — documented cases include renal complications from raw ingestion. Traditional lengthy cooking methods neutralize the acute irritation and toxicity risk, making properly prepared taro a safe staple food. One nuance worth naming directly: cooking addresses the acute raphide danger , but taro remains a genuinely higher-oxalate food even once cooked — soaking alone does not fully remove oxalate content. Anyone with a history of kidney stones should eat cooked taro leaf/root in moderation rather than assuming cooking eliminates the oxalate consideration entirely.

records.other_names: genip, guinep, chenet, mamoncillo — a beloved
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A widely loved Caribbean fruit, eaten fresh as a treat, with only modest traditional medicinal reputation beyond general nourishment.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 2, as food): A reasonably nutritious fruit with some antioxidant content; not a plant with significant medicinal research behind it beyond that.
records.preparation: Eaten fresh, the pulp sucked from around the large central seed.
records.cautions: The seed is a genuine choking hazard, especially for young children, given its size and smooth surface — a food-safety note worth including as plainly as any medicinal caution in this book.

records.other_names: golden apple, ambarella, June plum
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A tart Caribbean fruit eaten fresh, pickled, and juiced, valued primarily as food and a vitamin C source, with mild traditional digestive use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A genuinely good source of vitamin C and fiber .
records.preparation: Eaten fresh, ripe or green (often with salt and pepper when green, a common Caribbean preparation); juiced.
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone. No significant safety concerns identified.

records.other_names: rosemary; widely
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used across many traditions for memory, circulation, and hair health — rosemary oil rubbed into the scalp is a longstanding home remedy in Caribbean and Black hair-care tradition specifically.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Hair growth (Tier 2 — Promising): A small but genuinely encouraging body of clinical evidence supports topical rosemary oil for mild hair thinning, with at least one trial finding it comparable to a standard treatment. - Memory/alertness (Tier 2 — Promising): Some evidence supports mild cognitive benefits from aroma exposure and consumption.
records.preparation: Oil infusion for scalp/hair use; culinary use in cooking; tea.
records.cautions: Culinary and diluted topical use is very safe. Concentrated essential oil should always be diluted before scalp or skin application. High medicinal doses should be avoided in pregnancy and by those with seizure disorders.

records.other_names: holy basil, tulsi; entered
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Sacred in South Asian tradition and carried into the Caribbean through indentured Indian labor migration, tulsi became part of Indo-Caribbean home and spiritual practice alongside its use as a stress and immune tonic.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Stress/cortisol (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable and growing body of human trials supports mild stress-reducing (“adaptogen”) effects. - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some supportive evidence, not a treatment replacement.
records.preparation: Fresh or dried leaf tea; standardized extracts.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated. May have mild blood-sugar and blood-thinning effects — worth a doctor’s awareness if on related medication. Traditional caution around fertility-related use means it should be avoided in medicinal quantities during pregnancy.

records.other_names: lavender; broadly adopted into diaspora home
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Mediterranean in origin, thoroughly folded into modern Caribbean and Black American home wellness practice as a calming, sleep-supportive herb.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sleep & anxiety (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Genuinely solid clinical evidence, including for oral standardized lavender extract capsules used for mild anxiety.
records.preparation: Dried flower tea; diluted oil for topical/aromatic use; standardized oral extracts (the best-evidenced form for anxiety specifically).
records.cautions: Very safe as tea and diluted topical use. Undiluted oil should not be applied directly to skin. Oral lavender oil products should be used per product guidance, as concentrated oral use has different safety considerations than tea.

records.other_names: marshmallow root; adopted into Caribbean and African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Its mucilage-rich root was traditionally used to soothe irritated throats, coughs, and digestive discomfort — the origin of the confection’s name, though the modern candy no longer contains the plant.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Throat & digestive soothing (Tier 2 — Promising): The mucilage mechanism is well understood and plausible, similar in action to slippery elm; direct rigorous human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Cold-water infusion (draws out the mucilage better than hot water) or standard tea; lozenges.
records.cautions: Very safe for most people. Like slippery elm, it can slow absorption of medications taken at the same time — space other medications apart from it. Diabetics should note some traditional preparations include added sugar/honey and should account for this.

records.other_names: licorice root; widely adopted into diaspora herbal
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used broadly for soothing coughs, sore throats, and digestive upset (including historically for stomach ulcers) across many folk traditions absorbed into the American and Caribbean herbal shelf.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Cough/throat & mild digestive upset (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and some clinical support. - Reflux (Tier 2 — Promising, for deglycyrrhizinated licorice/DGL specifically): A specially processed form shows better evidence and better safety than whole licorice root.
records.preparation: Root tea; DGL (deglycyrrhizinated) lozenges and capsules for the reflux-specific use.
records.cautions: — A genuinely important, well-documented caution. Regular use of whole licorice root (not DGL) can raise blood pressure and lower potassium levels, sometimes seriously, especially with prolonged daily use. Anyone with high blood pressure, heart disease, or kidney disease should avoid whole licorice root and choose DGL products instead, and should avoid whole licorice entirely in pregnancy given traditional and some research-based concern about early labor .
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, for deglycyrrhizinated licorice/DGL specifically

records.other_names: ashwagandha; entered Caribbean wellness culture
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A cornerstone of South Asian traditional medicine, carried into Trinidad and Guyana through the same historical migration that brought fenugreek and holy basil, and now widely used across the broader diaspora wellness shelf as a stress and vitality tonic.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Stress & cortisol (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): One of the better clinically studied adaptogen-category herbs — multiple human trials support real reductions in stress markers and modest improvements in sleep. - Vitality/mild strength gains (Tier 2 — Promising): Some evidence of modest benefit when combined with exercise.
records.preparation: Standardized root extract capsules (the best-studied form) or traditional root powder in warm milk.
records.cautions: Should be avoided or used cautiously by those with autoimmune conditions or thyroid disorders, given evidence it can stimulate immune and thyroid activity. Avoid in pregnancy — traditional and modern safety data both counsel against it. May interact with sedatives and thyroid medication.

records.other_names: valerian root; broadly adopted into diaspora sleep-
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: European in origin, folded thoroughly into modern American and Caribbean herbal sleep practice as one of the most reached-for botanical sleep aids.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Sleep (Tier 2 — Promising, genuinely inconsistent on closer review): A widely studied sleep herb, but the evidence is weaker than this book first stated. A 2006 meta-analysis (16 RCTs, 1,093 patients) found a significant benefit on a simple “improved or not” measure, but the authors themselves flagged evidence of publication bias. More recent reviews using objective sleep measures (actigraphy, polysomnography) generally have not shown valerian outperforming placebo, with benefit appearing mainly on subjective self-report. One systematic review concluded evidence “did not support the clinical efficacy of valerian as a sleep aid” and suggested future research focus on more promising options. Corrected here from Tier 1 to Tier 2 to reflect this honestly.
records.preparation: Dried root tea (notably pungent smell) or standardized capsules.
records.cautions: Should not be combined with alcohol, sedatives, or sleep medication without medical guidance, given its own sedative action. Avoid in pregnancy. A small number of people experience the opposite effect (mild stimulation) — worth noting if that occurs.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, genuinely inconsistent on closer review

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Several Passiflora species are native to the Caribbean and Central America, and various forms have long traditional use across these regions for anxiety and sleep, alongside the plant’s broader adoption into general American herbalism.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Anxiety (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Genuinely solid clinical evidence, including trials comparing it favorably to standard anti- anxiety approaches for mild situational anxiety.
records.preparation: Dried leaf/flower tea; standardized extracts.
records.cautions: Generally very safe. Should not be combined with sedatives or sleep medication without guidance, given its real calming action. Avoid in pregnancy.

records.other_names: willow bark; the direct traditional-medicine ancestor of
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used across many traditions worldwide, including folded into American and Caribbean folk pain remedies, for fever and pain — its active compound, salicin, is the natural ancestor from which aspirin was chemically developed, making this one of the clearest plant-to- pharmaceutical stories in the Western herbal tradition, a mirror to periwinkle’s African/Caribbean parallel.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Mild to moderate pain (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Solid clinical evidence supports willow bark for mild-to-moderate pain, including back pain and osteoarthritis, working through mechanisms very similar to aspirin.
records.preparation: Dried bark tea or standardized extract.
records.cautions: — This carries essentially the same caution profile as aspirin, and should be treated with the same seriousness. Never give willow bark to children or teenagers with a fever or viral illness — like aspirin, it carries a risk of Reye’s syndrome in this population. Avoid with aspirin allergy, bleeding disorders, stomach ulcers, or blood-thinning medication. Avoid in pregnancy, particularly the third trimester .

records.other_names: feverfew; adopted into diaspora herbal tradition
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: European in origin, adopted into the broader American and Caribbean herbal shelf specifically for migraine prevention, a use that has held up better under modern research than many traditional claims in this book.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Migraine prevention (Tier 2 — Promising, genuinely mixed across reviews): On closer review, the evidence is more inconsistent than this book first stated. The Cochrane systematic review — the most rigorous body evaluating this claim — found results too heterogeneous to pool reliably; the one larger , well-designed trial showed a real but modest benefit (about 0.6 fewer migraine attacks per month than placebo), while several earlier and some more recent smaller meta-analyses have found effects ranging from modest and significant to statistically non-significant. This is a real, biologically plausible effect that has not yet produced the kind of consistent, high-quality evidence this book’s Tier 1 label implies — corrected here to Tier 2.
records.preparation: Dried leaf capsules (standardized extract) or fresh/dried leaf tea.
records.cautions: Should not be stopped abruptly after long-term use — some people experience a withdrawal-like rebound of headaches. Avoid in pregnancy, given real traditional and research-based concern about uterine stimulation. May interact with blood-thinning medication. Those allergic to ragweed-family plants should be cautious.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 2 — Promising, genuinely mixed across reviews

records.other_names: sugarcane; a plant whose plantation history is
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: No plant in this book carries a heavier historical weight — sugarcane cultivation was a primary economic engine of the slave trade, and its brutal plantation labor shaped the demographic and cultural map of the entire Caribbean. Alongside that history, the fresh juice and unrefined cane syrup were traditionally used as a nourishing tonic and energy source, distinct from the refined white sugar the crop is now best known for producing.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 2, for minimally processed forms): Fresh cane juice and unrefined cane products (like Caribbean “wet sugar” or Ethiopian/African brown sugars) retain some minerals lost in refining; refined white sugar carries none of this and is simply a caloric sweetener .
records.preparation: Fresh juice pressed and drunk immediately; unrefined syrup and brown sugar in cooking.
records.cautions: As with any concentrated sugar source, moderation matters for blood sugar , dental health, and weight management — this book does not recommend sugarcane products as a health remedy, only acknowledges their traditional and cultural place honestly, history included.

records.other_names: plantain; a starchy banana-family staple across West
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A foundational staple starch across West and Central Africa and the Caribbean, eaten green (starchy, savory) or ripe (sweet), and traditionally valued as an easily digestible food for the young, the elderly, and the recovering.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely nutrient-dense — potassium, vitamin C, fiber , and complex carbohydrates. - Digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Long traditional reputation as a gentle, easy-to-digest food, especially when cooked soft.
records.preparation: Boiled, fried, roasted, or mashed, at various stages of ripeness depending on the dish.
records.cautions: A very safe staple food. As a starchy carbohydrate, those managing blood sugar should treat it like any other starch — a matter of portion size, not avoidance.

records.other_names: sorghum; an ancient African grain, a staple across the
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Domesticated in Africa thousands of years ago, sorghum has fed and sustained communities across the continent’s drier regions, brewed into traditional porridges and fermented drinks, and valued for its resilience in difficult growing conditions.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A genuinely nutritious whole grain, naturally gluten-free, with good fiber and antioxidant content, particularly in darker-colored varieties.
records.preparation: Ground into flour for porridge and flatbreads; whole grain cooked like rice; fermented into traditional beverages.
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone, including those avoiding gluten. No significant safety concerns at ordinary dietary levels.

records.other_names: millet; another ancient African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Like sorghum, millet has sustained African communities for millennia in regions too dry for many other grains, ground into porridge, flatbread, and traditional fermented foods.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A nutrient-dense, naturally gluten-free whole grain, good source of magnesium and fiber . - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some evidence that whole millet may support steadier blood sugar response compared to more refined grains.
records.preparation: Ground into flour; cooked whole as a porridge or side dish.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. Those with existing thyroid conditions have sometimes been advised to moderate very heavy, exclusive millet consumption given some evidence of mild interference with thyroid hormone processing at high intake — a minor point worth a doctor’s awareness for heavy consumers, not a reason for ordinary dietary avoidance.

records.other_names: fonio; one of West Africa’s oldest cultivated grains,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Among the oldest domesticated cereals in Africa, fonio has fed West African communities for thousands of years and carries deep cultural and ceremonial significance in some Malian and Senegalese traditions, alongside its everyday role as food.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A nutrient-dense, naturally gluten-free ancient grain, good source of amino acids relative to many other grains.
records.preparation: Cooked like couscous or rice; ground into flour .
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone. No significant safety concerns identified.

records.identity: Citrullus lanatus var . or Cucumeropsis mannii (melon seed)
records.other_names: egusi; the
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The dried, ground seeds of a specific melon variety form the base of one of West Africa’s most beloved soups, valued traditionally as a rich source of protein and fat in the diet.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in protein and healthy fats, a real nutritional asset in traditional diets.
records.preparation: Ground into a paste or powder and cooked into soup with vegetables, meat, or fish.
records.cautions: Very safe as food. High in calories/fat, which is a nutritional asset in food-scarce contexts and a portion consideration in food-abundant ones — a matter of context, not danger .

records.other_names: bitter kola; a distinct West African tree, unrelated
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Widely chewed across West Africa, traditionally believed to ward off illness, support the liver , and ease coughs and throat complaints — culturally significant enough to be offered ceremonially in some Nigerian and broader West African traditions, similarly to true kola nut but botanically and traditionally distinct.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory & liver support (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable and growing body of laboratory research supports antimicrobial and liver-protective compounds; human clinical trials remain more limited than the plant’s popularity would suggest.
records.preparation: Chewed fresh or dried.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated in traditional amounts. Limited modern safety data for concentrated extracts — traditional chewing amounts are the best- supported form of use.

records.other_names: iboga; a Central African (primarily Gabonese) root
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Central to Bwiti religious and initiatory practice in Gabon and neighboring Central African regions for generations, used in structured, supervised ceremonial contexts by trained practitioners — this book includes it for honesty and cultural completeness, not as a remedy.
records.what_modern_research_says: - The claims: Iboga and its extracted compound ibogaine have drawn modern interest, including for addiction interruption, and some research exists on this specific application. - The overriding reality: This is one of the most potent and genuinely dangerous plants named anywhere in this book.
records.preparation: This book provides no preparation guidance whatsoever .
records.cautions: — The strongest caution in this entire book, alongside chaparral and comfrey, and more serious than either . Iboga and ibogaine carry a real, well- documented risk of serious and sometimes fatal heart rhythm disturbances, and deaths have occurred even in supervised settings, let alone unsupervised ones. Its legal status varies by country and it is restricted in many places specifically because of this risk. This book does not recommend iboga or ibogaine for any use outside of a licensed medical or closely supervised traditional ceremonial context with appropriate cardiac screening and monitoring, and includes this entry purely so that a reader encountering the name elsewhere understands the real gravity involved, not as an invitation to seek it out.

records.other_names: African nutmeg, calabash nutmeg, ehuru (Igbo)
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A West African spice seed used in cooking (particularly in Nigerian pepper soup) and traditionally for digestive complaints and postpartum recovery, distinct from true nutmeg though similar in aroma and culinary role.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional culinary-medicinal record; formal human clinical trials are very limited.
records.preparation: Ground seed used as a culinary spice, particularly in soups.
records.cautions: Well tolerated as a culinary spice in ordinary amounts. Limited safety data for concentrated medicinal use — culinary quantities are the best-supported way to use this plant, and postpartum traditional use should involve a midwife or doctor’s awareness rather than self-directed heavy dosing.

records.other_names: aidan fruit, prekese (Akan/Ghana), oshosho
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A distinctive four-winged pod used across West Africa, especially prominent in Ghanaian and Nigerian tradition, valued in cooking (soups and pepper soup) and traditionally for postpartum recovery, blood pressure, and general wellness.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood pressure & metabolic support (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely encouraging and growing body of laboratory and some animal research supports blood-pressure and metabolic benefits; human clinical trials remain limited.
records.preparation: Dried pod simmered into soup or a standalone decoction.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated in traditional culinary and tonic amounts. Anyone on blood pressure medication should mention regular use to their doctor given its real traditional and researched activity in this area. Limited safety data in pregnancy beyond traditional postpartum use, which should involve a midwife’s guidance on timing and amount.

records.other_names: coconut; a coastal African, Caribbean, and Indian Ocean
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Nearly every part of the coconut has traditional use across coastal Africa, the Caribbean, and the Indian Ocean world — the water as a refreshing and traditionally restorative drink, the oil for skin and hair and cooking, the meat as food.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Coconut water/hydration (Tier 1 — Research- Supported): Genuinely effective for mild rehydration, with a natural electrolyte profile that has real clinical support, particularly for mild fluid replacement. - Coconut oil (Tier “mixed/debated” for internal use, Tier 2 for topical): Coconut oil’s saturated fat content makes its internal, dietary health claims genuinely contested among individual researchers, but major health authorities (American Heart Association, British Heart Foundation, European Food Information Council) have reached a fairly clear consensus that coconut oil raises LDL (“bad”) cholesterol similarly to other saturated fats and does not offer unique heart benefits — a 16- study meta-analysis found it raised LDL more than most other oils tested. A common claim that its medium-chain-triglyceride (MCT) content sets it apart doesn’t hold up either: coconut oil’s dominant fat, lauric acid, behaves in the body like a long-chain saturated fat, not like the true MCTs used in the original MCT research. This book won’t pretend the case is more contested than it currently is. Topical use for skin and hair has more straightforward, supportive evidence.
records.preparation: Water drunk fresh; oil used in cooking and topically; meat eaten fresh or dried.
records.cautions: Coconut water is very safe for most people but those with kidney disease should be mindful of its potassium content. Topical oil is very safe; internal dietary use, like any saturated fat source, is reasonably a matter of moderation for those managing cholesterol — discuss significant dietary use with a doctor if you have heart disease risk factors.

records.other_names: cassava, manioc, yuca; a global staple food and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The starchy root is a foundational staple crop across West and Central Africa, the Caribbean, and Latin America, processed into flour (gari, farinha), fermented products, and countless traditional dishes, feeding more people daily than almost any other plant in this book.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as a properly processed food): A genuinely important caloric staple, though relatively low in protein compared to grains and legumes — traditional diets typically pair it with protein-rich foods for this reason, a sensible pattern worth naming.
records.preparation: Proper processing is not optional and varies by variety — bitter cassava varieties require extensive soaking, fermenting, grating, and cooking to remove naturally occurring cyanogenic compounds; sweet varieties require less but should still always be thoroughly cooked.
records.cautions: — A serious, well-documented safety matter , paired with this book’s earlier cassava leaf entry. Improperly processed cassava root, particularly bitter varieties, has caused serious cyanide poisoning outbreaks historically in communities relying heavily on it without adequate processing, and this remains a genuine public health concern in some regions today. Always follow proper traditional processing methods in full — this is one of the clearest cases in this entire book where tradition’s elaborate preparation steps exist purely because they are medically necessary.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: True yam is a foundational West African staple crop, celebrated with entire harvest festivals (the Yoruba and Igbo “New Yam Festival” traditions) — a food so significant it structures the agricultural calendar and cultural identity of many West African communities, distinct from the American “wild yam” covered earlier for its medicinal folk use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A genuinely nutritious complex-carbohydrate staple, good source of fiber , potassium, and vitamin C.
records.preparation: Boiled, pounded (into the beloved West African “pounded yam”), fried, or roasted.
records.cautions: A very safe staple food for virtually everyone. As a starchy carbohydrate, a portion consideration for those managing blood sugar , not a food to avoid.

records.other_names: groundnut, peanut, goober (a word itself derived from
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Though native to South America, the peanut became deeply African through cultivation and cuisine after early transatlantic exchange, becoming a foundational West African staple (groundnut stew) and crossing back to the Americas in enslaved people’s memory and language — the word “goober” itself is a linguistic fossil of that journey.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in protein, healthy fats, and various nutrients.
records.preparation: Roasted and eaten whole; ground into paste; cooked into stews.
records.cautions: — Two real flags worth naming plainly. Peanuts are one of the most common serious food allergens, and allergic reactions can be severe — this is a genuinely important safety consideration for any household. Separately, improperly stored peanuts can develop aflatoxin, a mold-produced toxin linked to liver damage and cancer risk with regular exposure — proper dry storage and discarding any moldy-looking nuts is a real food-safety practice, not an overreaction.

records.other_names: cowpea, black-eyed pea; a West African legume that
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Domesticated in Africa, the cowpea crossed the Atlantic in the same terrible journey as its people and became a cornerstone of Southern Black American cooking (hoppin’ John, and countless other dishes), carrying a whole food culture across an ocean in both crop and memory.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): A genuinely excellent source of plant protein, fiber , and folate.
records.preparation: Cooked into stews, soups, and rice dishes.
records.cautions: A very safe, nutritious staple legume for virtually everyone. No significant safety concerns at ordinary dietary levels.

records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Eaten fresh, juiced, and cooked into preserves across the Caribbean and broader tropics, valued simply and thoroughly as a favorite fruit.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Exceptionally rich in vitamin C — often higher than citrus fruit — along with good fiber content.
records.preparation: Eaten fresh, ripe; juiced; cooked into pastes and preserves.
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone. High fiber content means introducing large amounts gradually is sensible for sensitive digestion, as with any fiber-rich food.

records.identity: Mangifera indica (leaf, distinct from the beloved fruit)
records.other_names: mango leaf; a
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: While the fruit needs no introduction, the leaf carries its own separate folk tradition across parts of Africa, the Caribbean, and South Asia — brewed as a tea traditionally reputed to support blood sugar .
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): Some laboratory and preliminary human research suggests supportive activity; not established well enough to substitute for diabetes treatment or monitoring.
records.preparation: Dried leaf tea.
records.cautions: Anyone with diabetes should involve their doctor before adding this to a medication regimen, given potential additive blood-sugar-lowering effects. The ripe fruit itself is a very safe food for virtually everyone, a separate matter from this leaf-specific tea tradition.

records.other_names: pygeum, African cherry; a Central and East African
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Bark traditionally used across Central and East African highland communities for urinary complaints, later becoming the basis of a widely used pharmaceutical-grade extract for prostate health in Europe — a real African-to-global medicine story worth telling alongside periwinkle and willow bark’s parallels, though with its own serious complication.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Benign prostate enlargement (BPH) symptoms (Tier 1 — Research-Supported): Standardized pygeum extract has real, meaningful clinical trial support for easing urinary symptoms associated with an enlarged prostate.
records.preparation: Standardized bark extract (the studied and reliably dosed form); this book does not recommend informal bark preparation given the conservation issue below.
records.cautions: — A conservation caution as serious as any medical one. Wild pygeum populations have been severely overharvested to supply the global supplement market, pushing the tree toward real conservation concern in parts of its range. This book recommends sourcing only from suppliers using sustainably cultivated or certified bark, consistent with Part IV’s sourcing chapter . Medically, prostate symptoms should be evaluated by a doctor to rule out more serious causes before self-treating with any supplement.

records.other_names: sesame, benne — carried across the Middle Passage in
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: One of the clearest linguistic and culinary through-lines from West Africa to the American South — the very word “benne” is a preserved West African word, kept alive specifically in Gullah Geechee culture, a living monument to Part I’s Middle Passage chapter .
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in calcium, healthy fats, and various minerals — historically especially important as a calcium source in diets without much dairy.
records.preparation: Whole or ground seeds in cooking and baking; pressed into oil; tahini paste.
records.cautions: A very safe food for most people; sesame allergy, while less common than peanut allergy, is real and can be serious — worth awareness in any household introducing it to a child for the first time.

records.other_names: Scotch bonnet; the signature hot pepper of Jamaican
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Central to Caribbean cooking identity (jerk seasoning, countless hot sauces) and, like cayenne, put to traditional medicinal use for circulation and topical pain relief through its capsaicin content.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Topical pain relief (Tier 1 — Research-Supported, via capsaicin, shared with cayenne): The same well-documented capsaicin mechanism applies here as in the cayenne entry earlier in this book. - Circulation/ metabolism (Tier 2 — Promising): Similar modest supportive evidence to other capsaicin-rich peppers.
records.preparation: Cooked into food (used whole and removed, or minced, given its intense heat); occasionally infused into topical oils.
records.cautions: Extremely hot — always wash hands thoroughly after handling and avoid touching eyes or sensitive skin. Dietary use in sensitive individuals can aggravate acid reflux or ulcers. Topical capsaicin preparations cause a genuine burning sensation on first use that fades with repeated application — expected, not a sign of injury, but should be discontinued if it becomes genuinely painful rather than merely warm.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 1 — Research-Supported, via capsaicin, shared with cayenne

records.other_names: buchu; a Southern African shrub used for centuries
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used for generations by Khoisan and other Southern African communities for urinary tract discomfort, digestive complaints, and as an anti-inflammatory wash — one of South Africa’s oldest documented medicinal plants, later adopted into European settler pharmacopoeias too.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Urinary tract support (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable traditional and some laboratory support for mild antiseptic and anti- inflammatory activity; rigorous modern human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Dried leaf tea or tincture.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated in traditional amounts. Should not replace medical evaluation and treatment of a suspected urinary tract infection with fever or worsening symptoms. Buchu has documented uterine-stimulant effects — avoid in pregnancy rather than merely favoring caution, given this specific, real finding.

records.other_names: cancer bush,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A Southern African shrub with a very long traditional reputation as a general wellness and immune tonic, used for fever , stress, and as a supportive remedy during serious illness — the common English name “cancer bush” reflects historical folk use, not a proven modern claim.
records.what_modern_research_says: - General wellness/immune support (Tier 2 — Promising): Some laboratory and animal evidence supports anti-inflammatory and immune-modulating compounds; human clinical trials remain limited. - The name itself, addressed directly: There is no rigorous human clinical evidence that Sutherlandia treats or cures cancer . This book includes the plant specifically because its popular name causes real, harmful confusion, and will not let that name stand unaddressed.
records.preparation: Dried leaf tea or tincture, traditionally.
records.cautions: Should not be used as a substitute for cancer treatment under any circumstance. May interact with certain medications given its immune- modulating activity — anyone on immune-suppressing drugs or undergoing active medical treatment should discuss use with their doctor first, not after . A documented safety trial also found a possible interaction with isoniazid (a tuberculosis-prevention medication) that may reduce its protective effect — anyone taking isoniazid or other TB medication should not combine it with Sutherlandia without their doctor’s direct knowledge.

records.other_names: marula; a Southern African tree of deep cultural and
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The fruit has been gathered and valued across Southern Africa for millennia — fermented into traditional beverages, eaten fresh, and pressed for oil used on skin and hair — and the tree itself holds ceremonial significance in various Southern African cultures.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as fruit): Genuinely rich in vitamin C, among the highest of any commonly eaten fruit. - Skin use (Tier 2 — Promising): The pressed kernel oil has reasonable evidence of moisturizing and antioxidant benefit for skin.
records.preparation: Fruit eaten fresh or fermented; oil applied topically to skin and hair .
records.cautions: Very safe as food and topical oil for most people. No significant safety concerns identified at ordinary use levels.

records.other_names: sausage tree, kigelia; found across Southern and West
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Used traditionally across Southern and West Africa for skin conditions, wound healing, and as a topical treatment for various complaints — the fruit itself is not generally eaten but processed for its medicinal properties.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Skin conditions (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable and growing body of modern cosmetic and dermatological research supports kigelia extract for skin firmness and minor skin conditions — one of the more commercially validated African botanicals in modern skincare specifically.
records.preparation: Fruit and bark extracts prepared topically; traditional preparations vary regionally.
records.cautions: The raw fruit is not intended for eating — this is not a minor food-safety footnote. Consuming the raw, unprocessed fruit has been documented to cause severe vomiting and liver damage. Traditional processing for topical use should be followed rather than improvised. Patch-test any new topical preparation. Limited safety data for internal/oral use even when processed — this book does not recommend oral preparations of any kind.

records.other_names: waterleaf, gbure (Yoruba), mgbolodi (Igbo) — a West
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A soft, mucilaginous leafy green widely cooked across West Africa, especially Nigeria, valued as an everyday nourishing vegetable and traditionally for mild digestive and blood-supportive benefit.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely nutrient-dense — iron, vitamins A and C, and antioxidants.
records.preparation: Cooked into soups and stews, often alongside other vegetables.
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone. Contains some oxalates, like many leafy greens — a matter of dietary variety, not danger , for most people.

records.other_names: ewedu (Yoruba), jute leaf, Jew’s mallow — a
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Cooked into a distinctive, slightly mucilaginous soup across West Africa (ewedu soup is a Yoruba staple), valued as a nourishing everyday green much like okra in texture and traditional reputation for digestive comfort.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Nutrition (Tier 1, as food): Genuinely rich in vitamins, minerals, and fiber . - Digestive comfort (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Its mucilage plausibly soothes the gut, similar in mechanism to okra and marshmallow root.
records.preparation: Cooked into soup, traditionally chopped fine and simmered until it develops its characteristic silky texture.
records.cautions: Very safe as food for virtually everyone. No significant safety concerns identified.

records.other_names: leaf of life,
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A genuinely remarkable plant that grows new plantlets along its leaf edges, earning its “leaf of life” name — used traditionally for coughs, wounds, fever , and respiratory complaints, and considered one of the more powerfully regarded plants in Caribbean bush medicine.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory & wound support (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely encouraging and growing body of laboratory research supports anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds; rigorous human clinical trials remain limited relative to the plant’s traditional reputation.
records.preparation: Fresh leaf juice or crushed leaf applied topically; leaf tea for internal use in modest amounts.
records.cautions: — A real, less commonly known caution worth naming. The plant contains cardiac glycosides (compounds that affect heart rhythm) — well documented in veterinary toxicology from livestock grazing incidents — meaning large or concentrated internal doses carry real theoretical risk, particularly for anyone with existing heart conditions or on heart medication. Traditional modest use in tea form has a long safety record, but real moderation and a doctor’s awareness is warranted for anyone with heart concerns before regular internal use.

records.other_names: fitweed, culantro, shado beni, chadon beni — a
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A cornerstone flavor herb across the Caribbean (especially Trinidad, where it’s essential to green seasoning), and its folk name “fitweed” reflects a traditional reputation for calming seizures/ convulsions in children — a use this book flags honestly rather than endorses.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Digestive & anti-inflammatory use (Tier 2 — Promising): Reasonable laboratory support for digestive and anti-inflammatory compounds, consistent with its cousin cilantro/coriander . - The “fitweed” seizure- calming folk name (unproven — flagged directly): No rigorous modern clinical evidence supports using this plant to treat seizures, and a seizure disorder in a child or adult requires medical evaluation and treatment, not a folk remedy.
records.preparation: Fresh leaf used generously as a culinary herb; occasionally brewed as tea for digestive complaints.
records.cautions: Very safe as a culinary herb. Any seizure activity in a child or adult is a medical emergency or urgent medical concern — please seek immediate medical care rather than home treatment.

records.other_names: bitter bush, Christmas bush (in some regions), Siam
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Widely used across West and Central Africa and the Caribbean for wound healing — crushed fresh leaves applied directly to cuts and wounds to stop bleeding and promote healing, a genuinely widespread and consistent traditional first-aid use.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Wound healing (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable and growing body of laboratory research supports real wound-healing and blood-clotting-supportive compounds.
records.preparation: Fresh leaves crushed and applied directly to minor cuts and wounds.
records.cautions: Generally safe for minor topical first aid. Not a substitute for medical care for a deep, heavily bleeding, or infected wound. A separate, real finding applies specifically to oral/internal use (not the topical use described above): the plant contains pyrrolizidine-alkaloid-family compounds, and toxicology studies have found liver damage at higher internal doses — this book covers and recommends topical first-aid use only, and does not recommend teas, decoctions, or other oral preparations of this plant. Separately, this plant is classified as invasive in many regions outside its native range — a botanical/ecological note, distinct from its medicinal safety profile.

records.other_names: Spanish needles, beggar-ticks — an extremely widespread
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: One of the most widely used folk medicine plants across three continents simultaneously — African, Caribbean, and Latin American traditions all independently arrived at similar uses: wounds, digestive complaints, and inflammation, using a plant most people would otherwise dismiss as a roadside weed.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Anti-inflammatory activity (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely substantial and growing body of laboratory research across multiple countries supports real anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial compounds.
records.preparation: Fresh leaf poultice for topical wound use; leaf tea for internal digestive use.
records.cautions: Generally well tolerated for both topical and modest internal traditional use. As with any wild-foraged plant, correct identification matters — source from a known, clean area free of pesticide or roadside pollutant exposure.

records.other_names: sassafras; a Southern American root long used in Black
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Root bark traditionally brewed as a tonic tea across the American South, including within Black folk medicine, valued as a “blood purifier” and spring tonic, and historically the flavor base of traditional root beer .
records.what_modern_research_says: - Traditional tonic use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long traditional record; modern rigorous human trials are essentially absent given the safety concern below.
records.preparation: This book does not recommend home preparation given the caution below.
records.cautions: — A serious, well-documented safety flag. Safrole, sassafras’s primary active compound, is classified as a carcinogen in animal studies, and the FDA banned its use as a food additive decades ago for exactly this reason — modern commercial root beer no longer contains it. This book does not recommend regular consumption of sassafras tea or root preparations containing meaningful safrole content. This is a plant whose traditional reputation is real and whose modern safety data genuinely argues against casual home use.

records.other_names: pokeweed, poke salad, poke sallet; a defining
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Young pokeweed shoots, elaborately prepared, became a beloved spring dish across the Black American South (“poke salad” or “poke sallet”), and the plant carried traditional medicinal reputation for arthritis and skin conditions as well.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Traditional food use (Tier 3, food, only with correct preparation): A real and cherished culinary tradition when done correctly. - Medicinal use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): Traditional reputation for arthritis and skin conditions; modern clinical evidence is very limited given the safety profile below.
records.preparation: Only very young shoots are used, and traditional preparation requires multiple changes of boiling water to remove toxic compounds — this is not optional and varies by regional tradition, but the principle is universal: extensive parboiling is mandatory.
records.cautions: — One of the most serious food-safety entries in this book. Mature pokeweed — the roots, mature leaves, and berries especially — is genuinely toxic and has caused serious poisoning, including in children attracted to its berries. Even properly prepared young shoots carry some risk if preparation is rushed or incomplete. This book recommends real caution: only prepare this dish if taught directly by someone experienced in the traditional method, never let children have unsupervised access to the plant, and never eat the berries or roots under any circumstance.

records.other_names: boneset; Native American in origin, thoroughly
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Traditionally brewed as an intensely bitter tea for fevers and flu-like aches (the name reflects the bone-deep aching fever it was used to treat, not a fracture remedy), widely used across the American South well into the twentieth century.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Fever/flu symptom relief (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long, very consistent traditional record; modern rigorous human trials are limited.
records.preparation: Dried leaf and flower tea, traditionally taken warm and in modest amounts given its intense bitterness and mild laxative effect at higher doses.
records.cautions: Boneset itself (not just related plants) has been directly confirmed by chemical analysis to contain dehydropyrrolizidine alkaloids — the same liver- toxic compound family found in comfrey — across dried samples, tinctures, and hot-water infusions/decoctions alike. Researchers describe this as reason for “preclusive caution” pending further study of the actual carcinogenic risk. This book recommends against regular or long-term use, avoidance in pregnancy and breastfeeding, and avoidance entirely by anyone with existing liver disease.

records.other_names: yellowroot; an Appalachian and Southern
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: The bright yellow root was traditionally chewed or brewed for mouth sores, sore throat, and digestive complaints across Appalachian and Southern Black folk medicine, valued for its bitter , astringent properties.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Antimicrobial/astringent use (Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence): Contains berberine-family compounds, the same general class found in goldenseal and Oregon grape, with real laboratory- demonstrated antimicrobial activity; direct human clinical trials on this specific plant are limited.
records.preparation: Root chewed directly or brewed as a strong, bitter tea.
records.cautions: Berberine-family compounds should be avoided in pregnancy and used cautiously by nursing mothers. May interact with certain medications processed by the liver — moderate, occasional traditional use is the safest approach absent more research. A documented case report found chronic arsenic poisoning linked to a contaminated yellowroot tea product — a real reminder that wild-harvested or poorly sourced root products carry a genuine contamination risk; source from a reputable supplier rather than assuming all yellowroot products are equivalent.
evidence_tiers_detected: Tier 3 — Traditional Use, Tier 2 for some lab evidence

records.other_names: life everlasting, rabbit tobacco, sweet
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: Dried and either smoked or brewed as tea for coughs, asthma-like symptoms, and chest congestion across Southern Black folk medicine, valued as a gentle, sweet-smelling respiratory herb.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Respiratory support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use): A long, consistent traditional record; modern rigorous human trials are essentially absent.
records.preparation: Dried leaf and flower tea (the traditionally recommended form in this book, rather than smoking).
records.cautions: This book recommends tea preparation over the traditional smoking method, given the broader , well-established health concerns around inhaling any smoke, plant-derived or otherwise, regardless of the specific herb. Limited modern safety data otherwise; use in moderation.

records.other_names: curry leaf; entered Caribbean cooking and medicine
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A foundational South Asian culinary herb carried into Trinidadian and Guyanese cooking through indentured labor migration, and traditionally used medicinally for digestion and blood sugar , alongside fenugreek, tulsi, and ashwagandha as part of the same historical thread.
records.what_modern_research_says: - Blood sugar (Tier 2 — Promising): A genuinely reasonable and growing body of research, including some human studies, supports modest blood-sugar-supportive effects. - Digestive support (Tier 3 — Traditional Use).
records.preparation: Fresh or dried leaves used generously in cooking; occasionally brewed as tea.
records.cautions: Very safe as a culinary herb. Those on diabetes medication should mention regular concentrated use to their doctor given its real, if modest, blood- sugar activity.

records.other_names: amla, Indian gooseberry; entered Caribbean wellness
records.tradition_of_origin_and_historical_use: A cornerstone of South Asian traditional medicine, carried into Trinidad and Guyana, valued as one of the richest natural vitamin C sources known and a general vitality tonic.
